questions.stem: A pharmacology student is learning that pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics describe two different aspects of drug action. Which of the following statements best characterizes pharmacokinetics?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The biological and molecular actions the drug exerts on the body

choices.label: B
choices.text: The dose-response relationship of a drug at its target tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: The interaction of a drug with its specific cellular receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mechanism by which a drug produces its therapeutic effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: The time course of what the body does to the drug

explanation.summary: Pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug over time, summarized as ADME.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pharmacokinetics describes the time course of a drug in the body through absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME). It is often summarized as what the body does to the drug, in contrast to pharmacodynamics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The biological and molecular actions a drug exerts on the body define pharmacodynamics, not pharmacokinetics.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The dose-response relationship at the target tissue is part of pharmacodynamics.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interaction of a drug with its receptor is a pharmacodynamic concept.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The mechanism by which a drug produces its effect is pharmacodynamics.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman is prescribed estrogen for menopausal hot flashes. Her physician notes that when the drug is swallowed, a large fraction is inactivated in the liver before it reaches the systemic circulation. Which of the following medications would most likely undergo extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism?

explanation.summary: Orally administered drugs are absorbed from the GI tract into the hepatic portal vein and pass through the liver first, undergoing first-pass metabolism.
explanation.whyCorrect: After oral absorption, the drug travels through the hepatic portal vein directly to the liver, where drug-metabolizing enzymes can inactivate up to about 90 percent of the drug before it reaches the bloodstream. This first-pass effect lowers the bioavailability of oral drugs to an average F of about 0.7.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intramuscular drugs are absorbed from muscle into the systemic circulation and bypass the hepatic portal vein, avoiding first-pass metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intravenous drugs enter the systemic circulation directly, so they are not subject to first-pass metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Subcutaneous drugs are absorbed into the systemic circulation and do not pass through the portal vein first.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transdermal drugs are absorbed through the skin into the systemic circulation and avoid the first-pass effect.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A hospitalized patient requires a drug with an immediate and precisely controlled serum concentration, and the pharmacist selects a route that delivers the entire dose to the systemic circulation. Which route of administration has a bioavailability (F) of 100 percent?

explanation.summary: Intravenous injection delivers the drug directly into the systemic circulation, giving a bioavailability of 100 percent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because IV drugs are injected directly into the systemic circulation, 100 percent of the administered dose is available and F equals 1.0. IV administration also provides a rapid effect and a precise serum drug level.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inhaled drug bioavailability is reduced by absorption barriers and metabolic factors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intramuscular injection depends on absorption from muscle and does not reliably reach 100 percent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral bioavailability is less than 100 percent because of incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Subcutaneous injection must cross absorption barriers, so its bioavailability is less than 100 percent.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with angina is instructed to place a tablet under his tongue for rapid relief rather than swallowing it. Compared with the oral route, the sublingual route achieves a higher bioavailability primarily because it:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bypasses the hepatic portal vein and avoids first-pass metabolism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increases the fraction of drug bound to plasma albumin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Is absorbed across the large surface area of the alveolar epithelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Is broken down more rapidly by hepatic drug-metabolizing enzymes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uses an acid-resistant film coating that delays disintegration

explanation.summary: Sublingual drug is absorbed into venous blood of the oral cavity, which bypasses the hepatic portal vein and the liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: When placed under the tongue, the drug undergoes passive diffusion into the venous blood of the oral cavity, which bypasses the hepatic portal vein and the liver. Avoiding first-pass metabolism increases the amount of active drug reaching the systemic circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Increased protein binding would reduce the free active drug and is not the reason sublingual bioavailability is higher.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Absorption across the alveolar epithelium describes the inhalation route, not the sublingual route.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Faster hepatic metabolism would lower, not raise, bioavailability.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An acid-resistant coating delays absorption and is unrelated to why sublingual dosing avoids first-pass metabolism.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A drug circulates in the plasma in two forms: one bound to plasma proteins and one that is unbound. Which form is able to leave the bloodstream, distribute into tissues, and bind its receptor to produce an effect?

explanation.summary: Only the free, unbound drug can pass from the bloodstream into tissues to interact with receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: A drug in the bloodstream exists as free drug dissolved in plasma water and as protein-bound drug. Only the free, unbound fraction can pass from the bloodstream into tissues and interact with receptors to produce the drug's effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Albumin-bound drug is a specific form of protein-bound drug and is likewise inactive and confined to the circulation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A depot preparation is a formulation designed for slow release, not a plasma form of the drug.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metabolized drug has already been chemically processed and is not the active form reaching receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protein-bound drug is an inactive reservoir that remains in the bloodstream and cannot act on tissues.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with cirrhosis and hypoalbuminemia is started on a drug that is normally highly protein-bound. Compared with a healthy person, he is at increased risk of an exaggerated drug effect. Low albumin causes this risk because it:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accelerates renal excretion of the free drug

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreases the amount of unbound drug reaching the tissues

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increases binding of the drug to plasma proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increases the free, pharmacologically active drug fraction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduces the ability of the drug to cross the blood-brain barrier

explanation.summary: Reduced albumin lowers protein-binding capacity, raising the free active drug fraction and the drug effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: Albumin is the key plasma protein that binds drugs. Conditions such as liver disease and malnutrition decrease albumin levels, which lowers protein-binding capacity and increases the free, active drug fraction, leading to a greater or exaggerated effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A higher free fraction increases exposure and effect rather than speeding excretion in this scenario.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Low albumin increases, rather than decreases, the amount of unbound drug reaching tissues.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Low albumin provides fewer binding sites, so drug binding decreases rather than increases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Albumin level does not determine passage across the blood-brain barrier, which depends on lipid solubility.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman takes diphenhydramine for seasonal allergies and reports feeling drowsy afterward. This central nervous system effect occurs because diphenhydramine is lipophilic enough to:

choices.label: B
choices.text: Be excreted unchanged by the kidneys

choices.label: E
choices.text: Undergo complete first-pass metabolism in the liver

explanation.summary: The blood-brain barrier admits lipid-based drugs, so lipophilic diphenhydramine enters the CNS and causes drowsiness.
explanation.whyCorrect: The blood-brain barrier is a tight mesh of capillaries that protects the brain, and only lipid-based medications or those using a carrier can penetrate it. Diphenhydramine is lipophilic enough to cross the barrier and act on the central nervous system, producing drowsiness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Accumulation in adipose tissue is not the mechanism by which the drug causes drowsiness.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Renal excretion is an elimination process and does not explain crossing into the brain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Binding to plasma albumin would keep the drug in the circulation and would not produce a CNS effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Complete first-pass metabolism would reduce active drug rather than explain CNS penetration.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman is started on a lipophilic sedative, and her physician deliberately chooses a lower dose than would be used in a younger adult. Which age-related change most directly explains why older adults often require lower doses of such drugs?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Higher total body water than younger adults

explanation.summary: Older adults have more body fat, so lipophilic drugs accumulate and have a longer duration of action, requiring lower doses.
explanation.whyCorrect: Even at the same body mass index, older adults tend to have more body fat than younger adults. Lipophilic drugs accumulate in this fatty tissue, leading to a longer duration of action, which is one reason older adults often require lower doses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intestinal absorptive surface area does not increase in older adults; the elderly often have impaired GI function.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Higher total body water is characteristic of neonates and children, not older adults.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gastric emptying is typically decreased, not increased, in the elderly.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serum albumin decreases with age rather than increasing.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A patient with asthma uses an inhaler so that the drug is delivered to the lungs. Which property of the alveolar epithelium makes inhalation an effective route for drug absorption?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Its acidic pH that ionizes most drugs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Its complete lack of any epithelial or endothelial barriers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its direct drainage into the hepatic portal vein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its high concentration of plasma albumin

explanation.summary: The alveolar epithelium provides a very large surface area (about 100 square meters), allowing effective absorption of inhaled drugs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The alveolar epithelium is approximately 100 square meters in adults, providing a large surface area for absorption of inhaled substances. This large surface area allows drugs to be delivered effectively and even in small doses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An acidic ionizing pH is not the property that makes inhalation effective.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inhaled drugs must still cross barriers including the epithelial membrane, extravascular space, and vascular endothelium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The lungs drain into the pulmonary and systemic circulation, not the hepatic portal vein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Albumin is a plasma protein and is not a feature of the alveolar epithelium.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: Penicillin G is stable within a pH range of approximately 6 to 8. When it is taken by mouth, a significant portion is degraded before it can be absorbed. Which factor best explains this reduced absorption?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Degradation of the drug by the acidic pH of the stomach

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excessive lipophilicity preventing the drug from dissolving

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extensive binding of the drug to the alveolar epithelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immediate renal secretion of the absorbed drug

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rapid crossing of the blood-brain barrier

explanation.summary: The pH of the environment can impair drug absorption; acid-labile drugs like penicillin G are degraded in the stomach.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most drugs are weak acids or bases, and the pH of the environment can facilitate or impair drug absorption. Penicillin G is stable only within a pH of about 6 to 8, so the acidic environment of the stomach degrades the drug and reduces its absorption.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The problem with penicillin G is acid degradation, not poor dissolution from excessive lipophilicity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Binding to the alveolar epithelium relates to inhaled drugs and is irrelevant to oral penicillin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renal secretion is an excretion process, not a cause of reduced absorption in the stomach.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Crossing the blood-brain barrier is a distribution issue and does not explain reduced GI absorption.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes self-administers insulin into the fatty tissue just below the dermis rather than taking it by mouth. Which characteristic best explains why insulin is given by the subcutaneous route instead of orally?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It can only cross the blood-brain barrier when swallowed

choices.label: B
choices.text: It must undergo extensive first-pass metabolism to become active

choices.label: C
choices.text: It requires the 100 percent bioavailability that only oral dosing provides

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its large molecular size prevents effective absorption in the intestinal tract

choices.label: E
choices.text: Subcutaneous tissue is highly vascular and gives the fastest possible absorption

explanation.summary: The subcutaneous route is used when a drug's molecular size is too large to be absorbed effectively in the intestinal tract.
explanation.whyCorrect: Subcutaneous injection delivers the drug into the cutis below the dermis and epidermis and is used when the drug's molecular size is too large to be absorbed effectively in the intestinal tract or when better bioavailability is needed than the oral route. Insulin, heparin, and monoclonal antibodies are commonly given subcutaneously.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Crossing the blood-brain barrier is unrelated, and orally administered insulin would be degraded.
whyWrongByChoice.B: First-pass metabolism would inactivate the drug rather than activate it, and the subcutaneous route avoids it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oral dosing does not provide 100 percent bioavailability; only intravenous administration reaches an F of 100 percent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Subcutaneous tissue has few blood vessels, so absorption is slow and sustained, not the fastest possible.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A patient with severe peripheral atherosclerosis develops an infection in a poorly perfused lower extremity. Despite an adequate dose, the antibiotic is slow to reach the infected tissue. Which principle of drug distribution best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: First-pass metabolism has eliminated the antibiotic

choices.label: B
choices.text: High plasma albumin prevents the drug from ever becoming free

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduced blood flow limits delivery of the drug to the tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: The antibiotic is too hydrophilic to enter any tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: The blood-brain barrier is blocking drug entry to the limb

explanation.summary: Blood flow drives distribution, so blocked or reduced perfusion slows delivery of a drug to the affected tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blood flow plays a crucial role in the distribution of medications. Blocked vessels from atherosclerosis can hinder an antibiotic from reaching an infected area, so reduced perfusion limits delivery of the drug to the poorly perfused tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: First-pass metabolism affects oral bioavailability and does not explain poor tissue perfusion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no indication of elevated albumin, and protein binding is not the cause of the delayed delivery here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The problem is reduced perfusion, not that the drug is too hydrophilic to enter tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The blood-brain barrier only affects entry into the central nervous system, not a peripheral limb.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man swallows a tablet of an oral antibiotic. The drug enters the body and travels from the site of administration into the circulation. In which of the following sites does absorption of this drug primarily occur?

explanation.summary: Absorption, the first stage of pharmacokinetics, primarily occurs in the small intestine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Absorption is the first stage of ADME and occurs after a medication enters the body and travels from the site of administration into the circulation. For orally administered drugs, the primary site of absorption is usually the small intestine, with bioavailability influenced by the amount of drug absorbed across the intestinal epithelium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The esophagus is a conduit and is not described as a site of drug absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The large intestine is not the primary site of absorption for oral medications.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The rectum is the site of absorption for rectally administered drugs, not swallowed tablets.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The stomach is where acid-labile drugs may be degraded, but it is not the primary site of absorption.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man whose gout is controlled with probenecid is prescribed a cephalosporin antibiotic for pneumonia. His serum cephalosporin concentrations are higher than expected. Inhibition of which of the following processes by probenecid best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Active secretion into the renal tubules

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passive diffusion into the renal tubules

explanation.summary: Probenecid blocks the organic anion transporters (OATs) responsible for active renal secretion of drugs, decreasing excretion and raising blood levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Probenecid blocks the OATs that actively secrete drugs into the renal tubules for elimination. With renal secretion inhibited, the cephalosporin is excreted more slowly, resulting in increased drug levels in the blood.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Biliary excretion helps eliminate lipid-soluble drugs and is not affected by probenecid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: First-pass metabolism is a hepatic process affecting oral bioavailability and is not the mechanism of the probenecid interaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glomerular filtration is a form of renal excretion of unbound drug but is not affected by probenecid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Passive diffusion into the tubules is another route of renal excretion that probenecid does not inhibit.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: Routes of drug administration are classified according to whether the drug is delivered through the gastrointestinal tract or outside it. Which of the following routes is classified as enteral?

explanation.summary: Enteral routes (from the Greek enteron, intestine) are oral, oral mucosa (buccal), and rectal; all others are parenteral.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enteral routes deliver the drug via the GI tract and include oral, oral mucosa such as buccal, and rectal administration. Parenteral administration occurs outside the GI tract and includes IV, IM, intradermal, subcutaneous, transdermal, inhalation, otic, nasal, vaginal, and intrathecal routes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intradermal injection is a parenteral route, delivered outside the GI tract.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intrathecal injection into the spinal canal is a parenteral route.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nasal administration is listed among the parenteral routes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transdermal delivery through the skin is a parenteral route.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is given a drug formulated to be held against the inside of the cheek rather than placed under the tongue. Compared with sublingual administration, absorption from this site is expected to be which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dependent on disintegration in the stomach

choices.label: B
choices.text: Faster because the mucosa is more permeable

choices.label: C
choices.text: Limited by the drug's molecular size

choices.label: D
choices.text: Slower because the mucosa is less permeable

choices.label: E
choices.text: Subject to full hepatic first-pass metabolism

explanation.summary: Buccal tissue is less permeable than sublingual tissue, so buccal absorption is slower.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both sublingual and buccal routes deliver the drug by passive diffusion into the venous blood of the oral cavity. Sublingual tissue has highly permeable mucosa with rapid access to underlying capillaries, whereas buccal tissue is less permeable and has slower drug absorption.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Drugs absorbed through the oral mucosa do not need to disintegrate in the stomach.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The buccal mucosa is less permeable than the sublingual mucosa, so absorption is slower, not faster.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Molecular size limiting intestinal absorption is the rationale for subcutaneous injection, not the sublingual-buccal difference.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both oral mucosal routes bypass the hepatic portal vein and the liver, avoiding full first-pass metabolism.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl with fever cannot keep oral medication down because of repeated vomiting, so an antipyretic is administered as a suppository. Which of the following features of this route allows rapid and effective absorption of the drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct entry into the subarachnoid space

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passive diffusion into venous blood of the oral cavity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Slow permeation across the layers of skin

explanation.summary: The rectal route allows rapid, effective absorption via the highly vascularized rectal mucosa.
explanation.whyCorrect: The rectal route is an enteral route that allows for rapid and effective absorption of medications through the highly vascularized rectal mucosa. Drug absorbed in the rectum directly goes to the liver, but the route bypasses gut absorption and avoids the full effects of first-pass metabolism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Entry into the subarachnoid space describes intrathecal administration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The large alveolar surface area is the feature that makes the inhalation route effective.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Diffusion into venous blood of the oral cavity describes sublingual and buccal administration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Slow permeation through skin layers describes the transdermal route.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to place a peripheral intravenous catheter for a medication infusion and selects a vein in the forearm rather than one in the leg. The upper extremity is the preferred site primarily because it has a lower incidence of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Depot formation at the injection site

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protein binding of the infused drug

explanation.summary: The upper extremity is preferred for intravenous medication because it has a lower incidence of thrombophlebitis and thrombosis than the lower limbs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Peripheral veins, given their superficial location, provide easy access to the circulatory system for parenteral administration. The upper extremity is usually the preferred site for intravenous medication because it has a lower incidence of thrombophlebitis and thrombosis than the lower limbs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Depot formation describes intramuscular depot preparations, not intravenous infusion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erratic or incomplete absorption is a concern with oral dosing, not with direct intravenous delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intravenous drugs bypass first-pass metabolism regardless of which extremity is used.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasma protein binding is a property of the drug in the bloodstream and does not differ by injection site.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman requires an antibiotic whose absorption after oral dosing is known to be erratic and incomplete. The prescriber also wants the option of a depot formulation that releases drug over an extended period. Which of the following routes of administration is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: The intramuscular route is used when oral absorption is erratic or incomplete and allows depot preparations for sustained dosing.
explanation.whyCorrect: An intramuscular route is utilized when oral drug absorption occurs in an erratic or incomplete pattern. It can be administered into the deltoid, dorsogluteal, ventrogluteal, rectus femoris, or vastus lateralis muscles, and a depot preparation can be given intramuscularly to provide a sustained dose over a more extended time.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The ocular route has absorption limited to the eye because of physical barriers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The otic route is limited to ear disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sublingual dosing relies on the oral mucosa and is not the route used for depot preparations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transdermal delivery uses patches, ointments, or creams applied to the skin, not an injected depot.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with a chronic illness has difficulty adhering to daily oral dosing. He is switched to a depot preparation of his medication injected into the dorsogluteal muscle. Which of the following best describes the pharmacokinetic behavior of this preparation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diffuses rapidly into venous blood of the oral cavity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dissolves slowly into the circulation for a sustained dose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enters the systemic circulation directly for an immediate effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Permeates the layers of skin in a non-invasive manner

choices.label: E
choices.text: Undergoes degradation by stomach acid before absorption

explanation.summary: An intramuscular depot preparation dissolves slowly into the circulation, providing a sustained dose over an extended time.
explanation.whyCorrect: A depot preparation of a drug can be given intramuscularly, and the medication dissolves slowly into the circulation. This provides a sustained dose over a more extended time, which is useful when frequent oral dosing is impractical.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rapid diffusion into the venous blood of the oral cavity describes the sublingual route.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Direct entry into the systemic circulation with an immediate effect describes intravenous injection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Non-invasive permeation through skin layers describes the transdermal route.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stomach-acid degradation applies to acid-labile oral drugs, not an intramuscular injection.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman is discharged on heparin injections that she administers herself into the fatty tissue below the dermis. Which of the following best describes drug absorption from this site?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Delayed until the preparation disintegrates in the gut

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erratic because of variable muscle blood flow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rapid because the subcutaneous tissue is highly vascularized

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced by first-pass metabolism in the liver

choices.label: E
choices.text: Slow and sustained because the tissue has few vessels

explanation.summary: Subcutaneous tissue has few blood vessels, so injected medications are absorbed at a slow, sustained rate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Subcutaneous injections deliver drug to the cutis below the dermis and epidermis. Because subcutaneous tissue has few blood vessels, the medication undergoes absorption at a slow, sustained rate. The route is easy to administer and requires minimal skill, so patients can self-administer drugs such as insulin, heparin, and monoclonal antibodies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Disintegration in the gut applies to solid oral formulations, not injections.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erratic absorption related to muscle is not a feature of the subcutaneous route; muscle is the site of intramuscular injection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Subcutaneous tissue has few blood vessels; it is the rectal mucosa that is highly vascularized.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Subcutaneous drugs enter the systemic circulation without passing through the hepatic portal vein, so first-pass metabolism does not apply.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: An inhaled bronchodilator produces potent therapeutic effects at very small doses because of the large absorptive surface of the lung. The adult alveolar volume that provides this surface for absorption is approximately which of the following?

explanation.summary: The adult alveolar volume is 4,000 to 6,000 mL compared with an airway volume of 400 mL, providing a greater surface area for absorption of inhaled substances.
explanation.whyCorrect: The alveolar epithelium is approximately 100 square meters in adults, and the alveolar volume is 4,000 to 6,000 mL compared with the airway volume of 400 mL. This provides a greater surface area for absorption, so an inhaled route can administer drugs effectively and small doses can produce potent therapeutic effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 40 to 60 mL is far smaller than the stated alveolar volume.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This range corresponds to the airway volume of about 400 mL, not the alveolar volume.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This range is below the stated alveolar volume.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This range overstates the alveolar volume by roughly tenfold.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman applies a hydrocortisone cream to a localized rash on her forearm, intending an effect confined to the skin at the site of application. This route of administration is best classified as which of the following?

explanation.summary: The topical route produces a local effect directly on the skin, whereas the transdermal route achieves a systemic effect through slow absorption through the skin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some routes of administration help localize the effect of the drug to a specific area of the body. The topical route produces a local effect directly on the skin. In contrast, the transdermal route achieves a systemic effect through slow absorption through the skin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intradermal administration is an injection into the skin, not a cream applied for a local effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intramuscular administration is an injection into muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Subcutaneous administration is an injection into the tissue below the dermis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transdermal delivery is intended to achieve a systemic effect through slow absorption into the bloodstream.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A patient requires a drug to act directly on the central nervous system, and it is injected into the subarachnoid space of the spinal canal. Which of the following characterizes absorption by this route?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absorption limited by the physical barriers of the eye

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduced by first-pass metabolism in the liver

choices.label: C
choices.text: Slow dissolution from a depot in muscle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Slow permeation through the successive layers of the skin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Very fast absorption because the drug bypasses the blood-brain barrier

explanation.summary: Intrathecal administration is injection into the spinal canal or subarachnoid space to reach the CNS and has very fast absorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: The intrathecal route involves injection into the spinal canal or subarachnoid space to reach the central nervous system. Because the drug is delivered directly to the CNS, absorption is very fast.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absorption limited by physical barriers describes the ocular route.
whyWrongByChoice.B: First-pass metabolism affects orally administered drugs; intrathecal injection does not pass through the portal vein.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Slow dissolution from a depot describes intramuscular depot preparations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Slow permeation through the skin describes the transdermal route.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman is prescribed an antifungal medication administered intravaginally. The pharmacist notes that the drug may need to be dosed several times daily despite the high permeability of the tissue. Which of the following characteristics of this route best explains the need for repeated dosing?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Few blood vessels in the tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low permeability of the vaginal mucosa

explanation.summary: The vaginal route avoids first-pass metabolism and has high drug permeability but may require dosing multiple times daily because of the vaginal self-cleaning effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: The vaginal route avoids first-pass metabolism and has high drug permeability. However, it may require dosing multiple times daily because of the vaginal self-cleaning effect, which removes the drug from the site of application.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastric acid degradation applies to acid-labile oral drugs, not vaginally administered drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The vaginal route avoids first-pass metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Few blood vessels causing slow absorption is a feature of subcutaneous tissue, not the vaginal route.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The vaginal route is characterized by high, not low, drug permeability.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with glaucoma uses medicated eye drops daily. Systemic absorption of the drug is minimal, and its effect is confined to the eye. Which of the following best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Physical barriers of the cornea and conjunctiva keep the drug local

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drug accumulates in adipose tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drug is extensively bound to plasma albumin

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drug is inactivated by first-pass metabolism

choices.label: E
choices.text: The drug is too hydrophilic to cross the epithelium

explanation.summary: With the ocular route, drug absorption is limited to the eye because of physical barriers.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ocular route is used to administer drugs to the eye and helps localize the drug effect. Drug absorption by this route is limited to the eye because of physical barriers, so the systemic effect is minimal.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Accumulation in adipose tissue describes lipophilic drug distribution and does not explain a localized ocular effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plasma albumin binding affects distribution of drug already in the bloodstream, not local confinement to the eye.
whyWrongByChoice.D: First-pass metabolism reduces the bioavailability of orally administered drugs and is not relevant to eye drops.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Freely soluble hydrophilic drugs are described as having good systemic absorption; hydrophilicity is not the reason ocular absorption is limited.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A new drug is given to healthy volunteers by intravenous injection and, on a separate occasion, by mouth. Plasma concentrations after each dose are compared to determine the drug's fractional bioavailability (F). Which of the following best describes F?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fraction of the dose absorbed relative to intravascular administration

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fraction of the dose bound to albumin within the plasma compartment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fraction of the dose inactivated by the liver during its first pass

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fraction of the dose removed from the plasma per unit of time

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fraction of the dose that accumulates in adipose tissue over time

explanation.summary: F is the percentage of administered drug that enters the systemic circulation, expressed as extravascular absorption relative to intravascular administration.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fractional bioavailability (F) is the amount of administered drug that enters the systemic circulation, reported as a percentage from 0 to 100 percent. F is the percentage of drug absorbed from the extravascular route relative to intravascular administration, so it is affected by the route of administration, absorption, and other factors.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The fraction bound to albumin describes plasma protein binding, a distribution concept, not bioavailability.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The fraction inactivated on the first pass through the liver is first-pass metabolism, which lowers F but is not its definition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The fraction removed from plasma per unit time relates to clearance, which is covered in a later brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Accumulation in adipose tissue is a distribution phenomenon, not bioavailability.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: Two oral formulations of the same drug are given to a volunteer on separate days, and plasma concentrations are measured over time. Formulation X produces a markedly lower area under the curve (AUC) than formulation Y. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Formulation X binds more tightly to its receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formulation X has a higher bioavailability

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formulation X is more poorly absorbed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Formulation X produces greater systemic exposure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Formulation X remains in the circulation longer

explanation.summary: A lower AUC indicates poor drug absorption, rapid metabolism, or increased clearance, whereas a higher AUC indicates greater exposure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Plotting plasma concentration versus time allows calculation of the AUC, which shows how much drug reaches the systemic circulation and how long it stays there. A lower AUC indicates poor drug absorption, rapid metabolism, or increased clearance, so poorer absorption of formulation X is the most consistent explanation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Receptor binding is a pharmacodynamic property and is not measured by the plasma concentration-time curve.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Higher bioavailability means more drug reaches the systemic circulation, which would raise the AUC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Greater systemic exposure would produce a higher, not lower, AUC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A longer time in the circulation increases the AUC rather than lowering it.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man takes an oral medication. Pharmacokinetic studies show that the concentration of active drug begins to fall before the drug even enters the hepatic portal vein. Which of the following is the site of this initial loss?

explanation.summary: The first-pass reduction in an oral drug begins with metabolism in the cells of the intestine (gut wall metabolism) before the portal vein carries the drug to the liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: A drug administered orally undergoes a large reduction in concentration very soon after it is ingested. This starts with some metabolism in the cells of the intestine, and only after absorption from the GI tract does the hepatic portal vein transport the drug directly to the liver for further metabolism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The alveolar epithelium is the absorptive surface for inhaled drugs and is not involved in oral first-pass loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatic enzymes act after the portal vein delivers the drug to the liver, not before.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Albumin binds drug in the bloodstream and does not reduce drug concentration before portal entry.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The renal tubules are involved in excretion, which occurs after the drug has reached the systemic circulation.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is reviewing why oral drugs reach the systemic circulation less completely than intravenous drugs. On average, first-pass metabolism reduces the bioavailability of orally administered drugs to approximately which of the following values of F?

explanation.summary: First-pass metabolism reduces the bioavailability of orally administered drugs to an average F of 0.7.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the liver contains many drug-metabolizing enzymes, the concentration of active drug can be reduced by as much as 90 percent on the initial pass for some drugs. Across orally administered drugs, this first-pass effect reduces bioavailability to an average F of 0.7.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An F of 0.1 would correspond to the extreme 90 percent reduction seen with some drugs, not the average.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An F of 0.3 is well below the stated average for oral drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An F of 0.9 overstates the average oral bioavailability.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An F of 1.0 (100 percent) is achieved only by intravenous injection.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with acid reflux is prescribed omeprazole, an oral formulation manufactured with a special coating. Which of the following is the primary purpose of this coating?

choices.label: B
choices.text: To increase binding of the drug to plasma proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: To promote absorption across the oral mucosa

choices.label: E
choices.text: To speed disintegration of the tablet in the stomach

explanation.summary: Some oral formulations are coated with films that delay absorption; omeprazole has a coating to prevent stomach-acid-mediated degradation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Drug formulation in combination with the route of administration affects the rate of absorption. A solid oral dosage form must disintegrate and then be absorbed; some formulations are immediately absorbed, while others are coated with films that delay absorption. Omeprazole has a coating to prevent stomach-acid-mediated degradation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An oral coated tablet is still absorbed into the hepatic portal vein and does not bypass first-pass metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A film coating on a tablet does not alter plasma protein binding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The coated tablet is swallowed and absorbed in the intestine, not across the oral mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The coating delays rather than speeds disintegration, protecting the drug in the stomach.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant is given an oral medication, and the physician anticipates that absorption will differ from that in an adult because of incomplete development of organ systems. Which of the following age-related characteristics of infants best accounts for this difference?

explanation.summary: Infants have incomplete development of organ systems, including high gastric pH, decreased blood flow, and less intestinal absorptive area, all of which alter drug absorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: Age alters drug absorption. Infants have incomplete development of organ and biological systems, such as high gastric pH, decreased blood flow, and less intestinal absorptive area, all of which can change absorption of an oral drug.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Altered bacterial flora is listed among the changes seen in the elderly.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Decreased salivation is an impairment described in the elderly, not infants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased body fat is a distribution change of older adults; neonates and children have lower fat content.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Less gastric emptying is a feature of the elderly that alters absorption.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: Two oral drugs are being compared during formulation development. Drug X is freely soluble in water, whereas drug Y is poorly soluble. Based on drug solubility alone, which of the following is the expected difference in systemic absorption?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both drugs have equal absorption regardless of solubility

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drug X has better absorption because it is hydrophilic

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drug X has poor absorption because it is hydrophilic

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drug Y has better absorption because it is hydrophilic

choices.label: E
choices.text: Drug Y has better absorption because it is lipophilic

explanation.summary: Freely soluble drugs are hydrophilic and often have good systemic absorption, whereas poorly soluble drugs are lipophilic and have poor systemic absorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: The rate and extent of drug absorption depend on the drug's solubility. Poorly soluble drugs are lipophilic and have poor systemic absorption, whereas freely soluble drugs are hydrophilic and often present with good systemic absorption.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Solubility directly affects the rate and extent of absorption, so the two drugs are not expected to be equal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydrophilic, freely soluble drugs have good systemic absorption, not poor absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Drug Y is poorly soluble and therefore lipophilic, not hydrophilic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Poorly soluble, lipophilic drugs have poor systemic absorption, not better absorption.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man receives an intravenous bolus of a drug. Shortly after injection, drug concentrations are measured in several tissues. Which of the following tissues is expected to show the slowest initial distribution of the drug?

explanation.summary: Tissues with many blood vessels (lungs, kidneys, liver, brain) experience rapid distribution, while tissues with fewer vessels such as fat distribute drug more slowly.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tissue differences impact drug distribution. Tissues with a higher number of blood vessels, like the lungs, kidneys, liver, and brain, experience rapid distribution because of high blood flow. Tissues with fewer blood vessels, such as fat, have slower distribution, although lipophilic drugs tend to accumulate in adipose tissue over time in obese individuals.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brain is listed among tissues with high blood flow and rapid distribution, though barrier entry depends on lipid solubility.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The kidney receives high blood flow and distributes drug rapidly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The liver is a highly vascular organ with rapid distribution.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The lungs are highly vascular and experience rapid distribution.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with normal serum albumin is stabilized on a drug that is 95 to 98 percent bound to plasma proteins. He then begins a second drug that competes for the same plasma binding sites. Within days he develops signs of toxicity from the first drug. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accelerated first-pass metabolism of the first drug

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased passage across the blood-brain barrier

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased free, active fraction of the first drug

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased protein binding of the first drug

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced blood flow to the target tissue

explanation.summary: Competition for plasma binding sites displaces bound drug, increasing the free, active fraction and the drug's effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: For many drugs, the protein-bound portion accounts for 95 to 98 percent of the total drug in the bloodstream and is inactive while bound. Competition for plasma binding sites can impact the effects of drugs: when a second drug displaces the first from albumin, the free, unbound fraction that can reach tissues and receptors increases, producing an exaggerated effect even with normal albumin levels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Faster first-pass metabolism would lower active drug levels rather than cause toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced entry into the CNS would lessen, not increase, a drug's effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Competition for binding sites decreases, not increases, the amount of the first drug that remains protein bound.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nothing in the scenario suggests dehydration, atherosclerosis, hypertension, or heart failure altering blood flow.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A 3-week-old neonate receives a medication that rarely causes central nervous system effects in adults, but the infant develops marked sedation. Which of the following age-related distribution factors best explains the increased CNS exposure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Greater body fat causes accumulation in fatty tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Higher serum albumin increases the protein-bound fraction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lower total body water concentrates the drug in plasma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Slower gastric emptying prolongs intestinal absorption

choices.label: E
choices.text: The developing blood-brain barrier admits more drug

explanation.summary: In neonates and children, the developing blood-brain barrier allows more drugs to enter the central nervous system.
explanation.whyCorrect: In neonates and children, fat content is lower because of a higher total body water content, which results in decreased protein-binding capacity. In addition, the developing blood-brain barrier allows more drugs to enter the central nervous system, so drugs with little CNS effect in adults can produce sedation in infants.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased body fat with accumulation in fatty tissue describes older adults, not neonates.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neonates have decreased protein-binding capacity, and higher protein binding would reduce active free drug rather than raise CNS exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neonates and children have higher, not lower, total body water content.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Less gastric emptying is an absorption change described in the elderly and does not explain CNS penetration.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 of 3 - Drug Absorption and Distribution

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is asked to identify the body's principal site of drug biotransformation. Which of the following organs is primarily responsible for metabolizing drugs?

explanation.summary: The liver is the main organ of drug metabolism because it holds the highest concentration of drug-metabolizing enzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The liver contains a high concentration of drug-metabolizing enzymes, including the cytochrome P450 system, and is known as the body's 'detoxifying' organ. While other tissues have some metabolic capability, the liver performs the bulk of hepatic biotransformation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The kidneys have some metabolic capability and are the primary organ of excretion, but not the primary site of metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The lungs contribute only a small amount of drug metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The skin has minimal drug-metabolizing capacity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The spleen is not a significant drug-metabolizing organ.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: A drug given orally is absorbed through the GI tract and passes through the liver, where much of it is metabolized before reaching the systemic circulation. Which of the following routes of administration avoids this first-pass effect and yields the highest bioavailability?

explanation.summary: Intravenous administration bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism, giving the highest bioavailability.
explanation.whyCorrect: Drugs delivered intravenously enter the bloodstream directly, so they do not pass through the GI tract and liver before reaching the systemic circulation. This avoids the first-pass effect and produces the highest bioavailability.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Nasogastric administration delivers drug to the GI tract, so it too undergoes first-pass metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An oral capsule is also swallowed and subject to first-pass metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An oral solution is still absorbed enterally and passes through the liver first.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An oral tablet is absorbed through the GI tract and undergoes first-pass hepatic metabolism.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: Phase I biotransformation reactions modify a drug's chemical structure through oxidation, reduction, and hydrolysis. Which family of enzymes, located in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes, carries out these reactions?

explanation.summary: Cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes carry out Phase I oxidation, reduction, and hydrolysis reactions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phase I reactions are performed by cytochrome P450 enzymes located in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes. The name 'P450' reflects their peak light absorption at 450 nm, and they use heme as a cofactor to transfer electrons during oxidation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutathione-S-transferases mediate Phase II conjugation, not Phase I reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: N-acetyltransferases catalyze Phase II acetylation, a conjugation reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sulfotransferases catalyze Phase II sulfation conjugation reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: UDP-glucuronosyltransferases perform Phase II glucuronidation, not Phase I modification.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: Phase II biotransformation conjugates a drug with a functional chemical group to produce pharmacologically inactive metabolites that are easier to excrete. Which of the following is the most common Phase II conjugation pathway?

explanation.summary: Glucuronidation is the most common Phase II conjugation pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phase II conjugation adds an adjunct such as glucuronic acid, and glucuronidation is the most common Phase II pathway. It yields inactive, more polar metabolites that are excreted in the urine or feces.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glomerular filtration is a renal excretion mechanism, not a metabolic conjugation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydrolysis is a Phase I reaction, not a conjugation pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxidation is a Phase I modification reaction, not a Phase II conjugation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reduction is a Phase I modification reaction.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man taking a medication that is a substrate of CYP3A4 is started on ketoconazole, a potent CYP inhibitor, for a fungal infection. Which of the following changes in the co-administered CYP3A4 substrate is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased serum drug level with loss of efficacy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased renal excretion of the parent drug

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased serum drug level with a risk of toxicity

choices.label: E
choices.text: No change in the serum drug level

explanation.summary: A CYP inhibitor slows metabolism of its substrate, raising serum levels and toxicity risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: CYP inhibitors reduce enzyme activity and therefore decrease the ability to metabolize substrate drugs. The substrate has a decreased rate of metabolism and increased serum drug levels, which can lead to toxicity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Decreased serum levels occur with CYP inducers, not inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inhibitors decrease, not increase, the rate of hepatic metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The interaction alters hepatic metabolism, not renal excretion of the parent drug.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibition meaningfully changes the serum level by slowing metabolism.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: A patient stabilized on a medication that is metabolized by CYP450 enzymes is started on rifampin for tuberculosis. Rifampin is a CYP inducer. Which of the following effects on the co-administered drug is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased hepatic metabolism of the drug

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased serum drug level with toxicity

explanation.summary: A CYP inducer speeds metabolism of its substrate, lowering serum levels and efficacy.
explanation.whyCorrect: CYP inducers increase enzyme synthesis or activity, so substrate drugs have an increased rate of metabolism and decreased serum drug levels. Lower levels can reduce the drug's therapeutic effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inducers increase, not decrease, hepatic metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased serum levels and toxicity occur with CYP inhibitors, not inducers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Induction clearly changes metabolism by increasing enzyme activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Faster metabolism shortens, rather than prolongs, the half-life.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with hypertension and high cholesterol is started on verapamil and simvastatin. His physician advises him not to drink grapefruit juice while taking these medications. Grapefruit juice interacts with these drugs by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocking renal tubular secretion of the drugs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increasing first-pass metabolism of the drugs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inducing CYP enzymes, which lowers drug levels

explanation.summary: Grapefruit juice is a CYP inhibitor that increases the effects of simvastatin and verapamil.
explanation.whyCorrect: Grapefruit juice inhibits the CYP enzymes that metabolize simvastatin (a statin) and verapamil (a calcium channel blocker). By slowing their metabolism, it increases their serum levels and effects, raising the risk of drug-related side effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The interaction involves hepatic and intestinal CYP inhibition, not renal tubular secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Grapefruit juice does not act by enhancing Phase II glucuronidation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: By inhibiting CYP enzymes it decreases, rather than increases, first-pass metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Grapefruit juice inhibits, rather than induces, CYP enzymes, so it raises drug levels.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: Codeine itself has little analgesic activity; it must be converted by a CYP enzyme into morphine to relieve pain. A drug that is administered in an inactive form and requires metabolism to become active is best described as which of the following?

explanation.summary: A prodrug is a biologically inactive compound that must be metabolized to become active.
explanation.whyCorrect: A prodrug is administered in an inactive form and undergoes metabolism to be activated. Codeine is modified by a CYP enzyme into its active form, morphine, making it a classic prodrug example.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A conjugated metabolite is a Phase II product, typically inactive and ready for excretion, not an administered inactive drug.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A CYP inducer increases enzyme activity; it is not a drug that must be activated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A CYP inhibitor reduces enzyme activity rather than describing an inactive drug awaiting activation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A uricosuric agent increases uric acid excretion and is unrelated to the concept of drug activation.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: A patient with a serious infection is given probenecid together with penicillin so that the antibiotic remains at higher blood levels for a longer time. Probenecid produces this effect through which of the following mechanisms?

explanation.summary: Probenecid inhibits renal OAT transporters, decreasing tubular secretion and excretion of penicillin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Probenecid decreases renal excretion of drugs such as penicillins, cephalosporins, and methotrexate by binding to and inhibiting the organic anion transporters (OATs) in the nephron. This blocks their secretion into the renal tubules, keeping antibiotic levels higher for longer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Probenecid acts on renal transporters and does not block intestinal absorption of penicillin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mechanism involves renal tubular transporters, not biliary excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: It reduces excretion by inhibiting secretion; it does not increase glomerular filtration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Probenecid affects renal tubular transport, not hepatic CYP induction.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: Probenecid is also used to treat gout. It lowers blood uric acid by inhibiting tubular urate transport (for example, URAT1) so that more uric acid is excreted in the urine. This effect on uric acid handling is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It decreases urinary excretion of uric acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: It enhances hepatic metabolism of uric acid

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases tubular reabsorption of urate

explanation.summary: Probenecid is uricosuric: it inhibits tubular urate reabsorption, raising urinary uric acid excretion and lowering blood urate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Probenecid is a uricosuric agent that inhibits tubular urate transport, increasing the concentration of uric acid in the urine. This lowers the blood uric acid level and reduces gout symptoms such as joint swelling and pain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Probenecid increases, not decreases, urinary uric acid excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Its effect is on renal handling of urate, not hepatic metabolism of uric acid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: It inhibits urate reabsorption; it does not increase tubular reabsorption.
whyWrongByChoice.D: It acts on renal transport, not on the production of uric acid.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: During drug elimination, water-insoluble (lipophilic) metabolites are handled differently from water-soluble ones. Lipophilic drug metabolites are primarily excreted by which organ and route?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The kidney, into the urine by filtration

choices.label: B
choices.text: The liver, into the feces via bile

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lungs, in exhaled air as vapor

choices.label: D
choices.text: The salivary glands, in secreted saliva

choices.label: E
choices.text: The skin, in sweat from eccrine glands

explanation.summary: The liver excretes lipophilic metabolites in the feces, whereas the kidney excretes hydrophilic drugs in the urine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The liver excretes water-insoluble (lipophilic) drug metabolites into the feces, secreting them via bile into the gut. In contrast, the kidneys excrete water-soluble (hydrophilic) metabolites in the urine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The kidney excretes water-soluble (hydrophilic) drugs, not lipophilic metabolites.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The lungs account for only a small fraction of drug excretion, not the main route for lipophilic metabolites.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The salivary glands contribute only a small percentage of drug excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The skin is only a minor excretory route.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with hepatic cirrhosis is prescribed a drug that undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism. Compared with a patient who has normal liver function, which change is most likely, and how should dosing be adjusted?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased renal clearance; shorten the dosing interval

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prolonged drug half-life; reduce the dose

explanation.summary: Cirrhosis compromises hepatic metabolism, prolonging drug half-life and requiring a lower dose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatic diseases such as cirrhosis compromise Phase I metabolic pathways, so half-lives of drugs increase and the risk of toxicity rises. A decline in plasma proteins also raises the unbound drug fraction, so doses should be reduced to maintain the same therapeutic effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cirrhosis decreases, not increases, hepatic metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The problem is impaired hepatic metabolism, not increased renal clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cirrhosis lengthens rather than shortens the half-life, so increasing the dose would worsen toxicity risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Impaired hepatic metabolism does change drug handling, so an adjustment is needed.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: A lipophilic drug is administered to a patient. Over the next several hours, hepatic enzymes convert it into metabolites that are more polar than the parent compound. Which of the following best explains why this chemical change facilitates removal of the drug from the body?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Polar metabolites are converted into active prodrugs by the renal tubules

choices.label: B
choices.text: Polar metabolites are more readily stored in adipose tissue for later release

choices.label: C
choices.text: Polar metabolites bind more tightly to plasma albumin and stay in the blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polar metabolites do not cross lipid barriers and are excreted in the urine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polar metabolites have a prolonged duration of pharmacologic effect in tissue

explanation.summary: The goal of drug metabolism is to render the drug inactive and water soluble so it can be excreted in the urine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hydrophilic (polar) drugs and metabolites do not cross lipid barriers, so they are trapped in aqueous compartments and are easier to excrete. Water solubility allows urinary excretion through the kidneys, the most common route of drug excretion, and making the drug inactive prevents prolonged drug effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Prodrugs are inactive compounds activated by metabolism; the kidney does not convert polar metabolites into prodrugs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Storage in fat is a property of lipophilic compounds, and it would delay rather than facilitate removal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Drugs excreted by the kidney must be unbound from carrier proteins such as albumin; tighter protein binding would hinder, not facilitate, excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metabolism is intended to inactivate the drug and prevent prolonged effects, not extend them.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: A student learning about hepatic biotransformation asks why the Phase I enzyme family is called cytochrome P450. The name refers to which of the following properties of these enzymes?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A pH optimum of 4.50 in the endoplasmic reticulum

choices.label: C
choices.text: A spectrophotometric absorption maximum at 450 nm

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 450 isoforms identified in human liver

explanation.summary: The 'P450' designation refers to the wavelength, 450 nm, at which these enzymes show their absorption maximum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The term P450 refers to the spectrophotometric wavelength of 450 nm at which the cytochrome P450 enzymes are at their absorption maximum. It is a spectral property of the heme-containing protein, not a count or size.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The number does not describe molecular mass.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The name is unrelated to a pH optimum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The number does not refer to a count of isoforms; only a handful of isoforms are clinically important.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The number does not count substrate drugs; CYP3A4 alone metabolizes roughly half of prescription drugs.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: Cytochrome P450 enzymes carry out oxidation, reduction, and hydrolysis reactions, but oxidation predominates. Which of the following features of the CYP450 proteins best explains why they primarily transfer electrons?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are activated by covalent binding of substrate

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are anchored in the mitochondrial inner membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are synthesized only in response to inducing drugs

choices.label: D
choices.text: They require glucuronic acid as a cosubstrate

choices.label: E
choices.text: They utilize heme as a cofactor

explanation.summary: All CYP450 proteins use heme as a cofactor, which is why they primarily transfer electrons (oxidation).
explanation.whyCorrect: All CYP450 proteins utilize heme as a cofactor. Heme enables the enzymes to transfer electrons, so the characteristic reaction of the CYP family is oxidation of lipophilic compounds to alter or terminate their activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Covalent binding describes one way inhibitors block CYP activity, not the mechanism of electron transfer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CYPs are located in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes, not the mitochondrial inner membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CYPs are constitutively present; inducers increase expression but are not required for synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucuronic acid is a Phase II conjugation adjunct, not a CYP cofactor.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: In addition to metabolizing xenobiotic drugs, cytochrome P450 enzymes catalyze reactions in the synthesis of endogenous substances. Which of the following is an endogenous product whose synthesis depends on CYP proteins?

explanation.summary: CYP proteins help synthesize endogenous substances such as cholesterol, bile acids, vitamin D, and steroid hormones.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond drug detoxification, CYP proteins play an important role in catalyzing reactions involved in synthesizing endogenous substances like cholesterol, bile acids, vitamin D, and steroid hormones.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Albumin is a plasma carrier protein; it is not listed among CYP-synthesized products.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutathione is a Phase II conjugation adjunct, not a product of CYP catalysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemoglobin is not among the endogenous substances whose synthesis is attributed to CYP enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uric acid is handled by renal transporters such as URAT1 and GLUT9; it is not synthesized by CYPs.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: A pharmacist reviewing a hospital formulary notes that a single cytochrome P450 isoform accounts for the metabolism of approximately half of all prescription drugs. Which of the following isoforms is it?

explanation.summary: CYP3A4 metabolizes the largest share of drugs, about 50% of prescription drugs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the clinically relevant isoforms (CYP3A4, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP1A2, and CYP2D6), most drugs are metabolized by CYP3A4, which handles roughly 50% of prescription drugs. Inhibitors of CYP3A4 such as ketoconazole therefore affect many co-administered drugs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CYP1A2 is a clinically relevant isoform but does not account for half of prescription drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CYP2C19 is clinically relevant but not the dominant isoform.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CYP2C9 is on the must-know list but metabolizes a smaller share than CYP3A4.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CYP2D6 is important for opioid responsiveness but is not the isoform responsible for about 50% of drugs.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with acid reflux is prescribed a proton pump inhibitor. The drug is administered in a biologically inactive form and must undergo chemical reactions in the body before it can suppress gastric acid. Which of the following drugs is she most likely taking?

explanation.summary: Omeprazole, an acid reflux drug, is a prodrug that is activated after it undergoes chemical reactions.
explanation.whyCorrect: A prodrug is a biologically inactive compound that undergoes metabolism to be activated. Omeprazole, used for acid reflux, is a common example: it is activated only after it goes through chemical reactions. Omeprazole is also listed as a CYP inhibitor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic CYP inhibitor, not an acid reflux drug.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbamazepine is an anticonvulsant CYP inducer, not a proton pump inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cobicistat is an antiretroviral CYP inhibitor used in HIV treatment, not an acid reflux drug.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cyclosporin is an immunosuppressant and CYP inhibitor, not a proton pump inhibitor or prodrug in this context.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: A drug undergoes Phase II conjugation in a hepatocyte. Which of the following best describes the pharmacologic activity and fate of the resulting products?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Active metabolites that are reabsorbed across the renal tubules

choices.label: B
choices.text: Active metabolites that are stored in the liver until needed

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inactive metabolites that are polar (urine) or nonpolar (feces)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inactive metabolites that must be oxidized before excretion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prodrugs that are activated by intestinal bacteria

explanation.summary: Phase II conjugation yields two types of pharmacologically inactive metabolites: polar ones excreted in urine and nonpolar ones eliminated in feces.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phase II conjugation, carried out most commonly by hepatic transferase enzymes, adds a functional chemical group to the drug and results in pharmacologically inactive metabolites. These are either polar (water soluble) molecules excreted in the urine or nonpolar molecules eliminated in the feces.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conjugates are inactive; tubular back-diffusion is a property of some unconjugated drugs, not the defining fate of Phase II products.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Conjugated products are inactive and are eliminated, not stored as active drug.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxidation is a Phase I reaction; when needed it precedes conjugation, not the reverse.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Conjugation inactivates drugs; it does not create prodrugs.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: A newly developed drug is found to be a poor substrate for hepatic transferase enzymes until it has first been oxidized by a cytochrome P450 enzyme. Which of the following statements about hepatic biotransformation best accounts for this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conjugation reactions occur only in the kidney, not the liver

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oxidation is itself a Phase II conjugation reaction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phase II conjugation must always precede Phase I modification

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some drugs require Phase I modification before Phase II conjugation can occur

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transferase enzymes and CYP enzymes act on the same active site simultaneously

explanation.summary: Drugs can enter Phase II directly or after Phase I, and sometimes Phase I must happen before Phase II can occur.
explanation.whyCorrect: Drugs can enter Phase II reactions directly or after Phase I biotransformation. For some drugs, a Phase I modification (oxidation, reduction, or hydrolysis) must occur first so that a functional group is available for the transferase enzymes to conjugate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phase II reactions occur in the liver, kidneys, lungs, intestines, and other organs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oxidation is a Phase I modification reaction, not a conjugation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The order is the reverse: when a sequence is required, Phase I precedes Phase II.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phase I is performed by CYP enzymes and Phase II by transferase enzymes; they are distinct steps, not a single simultaneous event.

questions.topicName: Pharmacokinetics 1 (2 of 3): Drug Metabolism and Excretion

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department in hemorrhagic shock after a motor vehicle collision. He is hypotensive and hypovolemic. Compared with a hemodynamically stable patient, which of the following changes in the handling of a hepatically metabolized drug is most likely in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased rate of hepatic metabolism due to reduced liver perfusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased Phase II conjugation due to greater substrate delivery

choices.label: C
