whyWrongByChoice.A: Efficacy reflects the maximal effect (Emax), which is stated to be equal for both drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both drugs share the same maximal effect, so neither has greater efficacy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Drug Y has the higher EC50, so it needs more drug and is less potent, not more potent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Different EC50 values (1 nM vs 100 nM) mean the drugs differ in potency.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: On a graded dose-response curve, drug A plateaus at a higher maximal effect than drug B even at saturating concentrations. This indicates that drug A has greater which of the following?

explanation.summary: The height of the maximal-effect plateau (Emax) reflects efficacy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Efficacy is a measure of the maximal response produced by a drug, read as the Emax plateau of the curve. A drug whose curve plateaus at a higher Emax has greater efficacy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Affinity is how tightly the drug binds its receptor and is not read as the plateau height.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Potency relates to the EC50 (amount of drug needed), not to the height of the plateau.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Selectivity refers to producing one main effect at an appropriately high concentration, not maximal effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Specificity means having a single effect across all biological systems, unrelated to Emax.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A student plots the same dose-response data two ways: once with drug concentration on a linear scale and once on a semi-logarithmic scale. Which of the following correctly describes the shapes obtained?

choices.label: D
choices.text: The linear-scale plot is hyperbolic and the semi-log plot is sigmoidal

choices.label: E
choices.text: The linear-scale plot is sigmoidal and the semi-log plot is hyperbolic

explanation.summary: Plotted linearly a dose-response curve is hyperbolic; plotted on a semi-log scale it becomes sigmoidal (S-shaped).
explanation.whyCorrect: On a linear scale the dose-response relationship is hyperbolic, reaching a maximum at high concentrations because of receptor saturation. On a semi-log scale (log concentration vs effect) it becomes sigmoidal, which is preferred because it makes the EC50 easier to determine accurately.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The semi-log plot is sigmoidal, not hyperbolic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The linear-scale plot is hyperbolic, not sigmoidal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neither plot is a straight line; both are curved.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The shapes are reversed: linear gives the hyperbola and semi-log gives the sigmoid.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: The potency of a drug is commonly quantified using its EC50. The EC50 is best defined as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The concentration that produces 50% of the maximal effect

choices.label: B
choices.text: The concentration that saturates all available receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: The dose that produces a toxic effect in 50% of subjects

choices.label: D
choices.text: The fraction of receptors bound at equilibrium

choices.label: E
choices.text: The maximal effect the drug can produce

explanation.summary: EC50 is the concentration producing 50% of the maximal (half-maximal) effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines EC50 as the concentration that produces 50% of Emax, or the drug's half-maximal effect. It is used to determine potency and is best read on the linear portion of the curve.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Saturation of all receptors occurs at high concentrations that give the plateau, not at the half-maximal point.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A toxic effect in 50% of subjects describes a toxic dose, not the EC50 for effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The fraction of receptors bound relates to affinity/occupancy, not to the definition of EC50.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The maximal effect is Emax (efficacy), not EC50.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: Albuterol binds the beta-2 adrenergic receptor with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 100 nM. Compared with a second drug that binds the same receptor with a Kd of 10 nM, albuterol has which of the following?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Greater potency because of its higher Kd

choices.label: C
choices.text: Higher affinity because its Kd is higher

choices.label: E
choices.text: The same affinity as the second drug

explanation.summary: A higher Kd reflects weaker binding and therefore lower affinity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Affinity is inversely proportional to Kd (affinity = 1/Kd). A higher Kd value means weaker binding and lower affinity. Albuterol's Kd of 100 nM is higher than the other drug's 10 nM, so albuterol binds the beta-2 receptor with lower affinity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Kd reflects binding strength, not the maximal effect that defines efficacy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lower affinity tends to raise EC50 and lower potency, so a higher Kd does not increase potency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A higher Kd means lower, not higher, affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The Kd values differ (100 nM vs 10 nM), so the affinities are not the same.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A patient with tachycardia is treated with a beta-blocker chosen to act on beta-1 receptors while largely sparing beta-2 receptors. Which of the following drugs best fits this selective beta-1 blocking profile?

explanation.summary: Metoprolol is a selective beta-1 blocker used for an increased heart rate.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes metoprolol as a selective beta-1 blocker, used in cases of increased heart rate (tachycardia), whereas propranolol is non-selective. Metoprolol therefore fits a beta-1-selective profile.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Albuterol is a beta-2 agonist, not a beta-blocker.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aspirin reduces clotting and is unrelated to beta-adrenergic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lisinopril is a hypertension medication, not a beta-blocker.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker that blocks both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A drug that produced only one effect across all biological systems would be called specific, but in reality most drugs produce one main effect only at an appropriately high concentration. This more realistic property is termed which of the following?

explanation.summary: Selectivity is producing one main effect at an appropriately high concentration; specificity (a single effect on all systems) is rarely achieved.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick distinguishes specificity (one effect on all biological systems) from selectivity. Because the vast majority of drugs are selective rather than specific, producing their effect at an appropriately high concentration, the described property is selectivity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Affinity is the extent to which a drug binds its receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Efficacy is the maximal response a drug can produce.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Potency is the amount of drug needed to reach an established effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Specificity means a single effect across all systems, which the stem says is rarely achieved.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A patient takes an antacid to neutralize gastric acid. Applying the concept of a drug's effect as the downstream consequence of a drug-target interaction, the expected result is which of the following?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Activation of beta-2 receptors in the lungs

explanation.summary: Neutralizing stomach acid raises stomach pH; this is the downstream drug effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: A drug's effect describes the downstream consequences of a drug-target interaction. The brick uses the example that a drug that neutralizes stomach acid should have the effect of increasing stomach pH.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Decreasing G-protein activity is another separate example, not the effect of neutralizing stomach acid.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neutralizing acid raises pH; it does not lower it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Activating beta-2 receptors is the mechanism of a bronchodilator, a separate example unrelated to gastric acid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibiting dopamine receptors is a different example used to illustrate decreased receptor activity.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with hypertension and a myocardial infarction 5 years ago is scheduled for minor knee surgery. His medications are lisinopril, metoprolol, and aspirin. The surgical resident explains that one medication should be stopped about 7 days before surgery to reduce the risk of excessive bleeding. Which medication should be stopped?

choices.label: E
choices.text: None of his medications need to be stopped

explanation.summary: Aspirin reduces clotting and increases bleeding risk, so it is held roughly 7 days before surgery.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the case, aspirin is taken to reduce clotting risk but can increase the risk of bleeding. It is stopped about 1 week (7 days) before surgery and restarted post-discharge, so aspirin is the medication to hold.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Neither lisinopril nor metoprolol is the antiplatelet agent; only aspirin affects clotting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lisinopril treats his hypertension and is not the source of the bleeding risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metoprolol controls his heart rate and does not drive the bleeding risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aspirin does increase bleeding risk and needs to be held before surgery.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: Receptors that a drug may bind include G-protein-coupled receptors, tyrosine kinase (catalytic) receptors, and nuclear receptors. A molecule, whether produced by the body or introduced from outside it, that binds to such a receptor is termed which of the following?

explanation.summary: A ligand is a molecule that binds a receptor and may be endogenous or exogenous.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines a ligand as a molecule that binds to a receptor and notes that ligands can be endogenous or exogenous to the body. Agonists and antagonists are both ligands.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The dissociation constant (Kd) is a measure of binding strength, not a molecule.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Emax is the maximal effect of a drug, not a binding molecule.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A substrate is bound and converted by an enzyme; a ligand is defined by binding a receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A second messenger acts downstream inside the cell, not as the receptor-binding molecule.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A pharmacology course opens by summarizing one branch of the discipline as 'what the drug does to the body.' It is further described as the relationship of drug concentration at the site of action to the resulting therapeutic and adverse effects, including how much drug is required to achieve a desired effect. This branch is best termed which of the following?

explanation.summary: Pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body: the relationship of drug concentration at the site of action to its therapeutic and adverse effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines pharmacodynamics as what the drug does to the body. It includes the relationship of drug concentration at the site of action to therapeutic and adverse effects, and how much drug is required to achieve the desired effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bioavailability is a single measure of drug reaching the circulation, not a branch describing drug effects on the body.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pharmacogenomics deals with genetic influences on drug response, not the general concentration-effect relationship described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pharmacokinetics concerns what the body does to the drug, not the concentration-effect relationship at the site of action.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxicology focuses on harmful effects and is narrower than the description, which includes therapeutic effects.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A hospitalized patient is given a dose of bicarbonate, and the pH of the body compartment into which it distributes rises. Which of the following best describes how this drug produces its effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activates a G-protein-coupled receptor on the cell surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alters the chemical conditions inside the body by adding a base

choices.label: D
choices.text: Binds a nuclear receptor and sets off a cascade of cellular changes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Competes with an endogenous ligand for its receptor binding site

explanation.summary: Some drugs act not by binding a receptor but by altering the chemical conditions inside the body, such as bicarbonate adding a base.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that a drug might bind a target such as a receptor to set off a cascade of cellular changes, or it might alter the chemical conditions inside the body, giving the example of adding a base such as bicarbonate. Bicarbonate therefore acts by changing chemical conditions rather than through a receptor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: G-protein-coupled receptor activation is a receptor-mediated cascade, which is the contrasting mechanism the brick distinguishes from bicarbonate's action.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tyrosine kinase receptor activation is a receptor-mediated mechanism; bicarbonate does not act through a receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nuclear receptor binding is a receptor-mediated mechanism; bicarbonate acts by changing chemical conditions, not by binding a receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Competing for a receptor binding site describes an antagonist, not a base that alters body chemistry.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: In explaining how a drug elicits its effects, a pharmacologist describes the component of the cell that interacts with the drug and initiates the chain of events leading to the drug's observed effects. This component is defined as a protein that recognizes a signaling molecule endogenous to the cell and translates it into a functional cellular event. Which of the following terms applies?

explanation.summary: A receptor is the cellular component that interacts with a drug and initiates the chain of events leading to its effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that a drug must bind to a component of the organism, which pharmacologists usually call a receptor. Receptors are defined as proteins that recognize an endogenous signaling molecule and translate it into a functional cellular event, initiating the chain of events leading to the drug's observed effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An agonist is a ligand that activates a receptor; it is not the recognizing protein itself.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A substrate is acted on by an enzyme; the description is of a signal-recognizing protein, not a substrate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A ligand is the molecule that binds the receptor, not the protein that recognizes it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A second messenger acts downstream of the receptor and does not itself recognize the signaling molecule.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A researcher classifies the receptor targets of several drugs. One drug binds a receptor described as enzyme-linked, or catalytic. Which of the following receptor types best fits this description?

explanation.summary: Tyrosine kinase receptors are the enzyme-linked (catalytic) receptor class.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists receptor types as G-protein-coupled receptors, enzyme-linked (i.e., catalytic) receptors such as tyrosine kinase receptors, other membrane-associated receptors, and nuclear receptors. The enzyme-linked or catalytic class is represented by tyrosine kinase receptors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A G protein is a signaling component whose activity changes downstream of receptor activation; it is not a receptor type.
whyWrongByChoice.B: G-protein-coupled receptors are listed as a separate class from the enzyme-linked (catalytic) receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Other membrane-associated receptors are listed separately from the enzyme-linked class.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nuclear receptors are a distinct class and are not described as catalytic.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A candidate compound is tested on cells expressing a receptor for an endogenous neurotransmitter. Applied alone, the compound binds the receptor but produces no measurable cellular response. When the neurotransmitter is then added, its usual response is prevented for as long as the compound is present. Which of the following best classifies the compound?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A non-ligand, since no response occurred

explanation.summary: A molecule that binds a receptor, produces no effect itself, and blocks the endogenous ligand's action is an antagonist.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's figure shows an antagonist bound to the receptor with 'no effect,' in contrast to a ligand or agonist that produces an effect. Antagonists block a receptor's function and its associated cellular action by binding or competing for binding, which is exactly what the compound does when it prevents the neurotransmitter's response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A ligand is any molecule that binds a receptor; antagonists are ligands even though they produce no effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An agonist binds and activates the receptor, producing a cellular action; this compound produces none.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The compound is a test substance introduced from outside, and the endogenous ligand in the experiment is the neurotransmitter.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A second messenger acts downstream inside the cell; it does not bind the receptor from the outside and block the neurotransmitter.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A drug's response is plotted against its concentration on a linear scale. The curve rises steeply at low concentrations, then flattens and approaches a maximum despite further increases in concentration. Which of the following best explains the plateau?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A change in the plotting scale from linear to logarithmic

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion of the drug to an inactive form at high doses

choices.label: C
choices.text: Depletion of the endogenous ligand from the tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of the drug's affinity for the receptor at high doses

choices.label: E
choices.text: Saturation of the available receptors by the drug

explanation.summary: On a linear scale the dose-response curve is hyperbolic and reaches a maximum because available receptors become saturated.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that a dose-response relationship plotted on a linear scale is hyperbolic and that at high concentrations the response reaches a maximum due to saturation of available receptors by the drug, as also discussed in enzyme kinetics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The scale is stated to be linear; the plateau is a feature of the biology, not of the plotting method.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The plateau reflects receptor saturation, not inactivation of the drug at high doses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The plateau is explained by receptor occupancy by the drug, not by running out of endogenous ligand.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Affinity is a property of the drug-receptor interaction and does not fall as the dose rises.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: Two students plot the same dose-response data. One uses drug concentration on a linear x axis and obtains a hyperbolic curve; the other uses the logarithm of drug concentration and obtains a sigmoidal curve. The course director states that the second plot is the preferred method. Which of the following is the primary reason?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It converts the response into a straight line

choices.label: B
choices.text: It eliminates receptor saturation at high concentrations

choices.label: C
choices.text: It makes the EC50 easier to determine accurately

choices.label: D
choices.text: It raises the Emax that the drug can reach

choices.label: E
choices.text: It reveals the dissociation constant directly

explanation.summary: The semi-log plot is preferred because it makes the EC50 easier to determine accurately.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the semi-log plot (logarithm of drug concentration vs effect) is the preferred method for plotting dose-response relationships because it becomes easier to accurately determine the EC50 value, the concentration producing 50% of the maximum response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The semi-log plot yields a sigmoidal (S-shaped) curve, not a straight line.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Receptor saturation still occurs; changing the axis does not alter the biology of the plateau.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The maximal effect (Emax) is a property of the drug and is unchanged by how the data are plotted.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The semi-log dose-response plot is used to read EC50; it does not directly give the Kd.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A student estimates a drug's EC50 from a semi-log dose-response curve by reading the concentration at the point where the curve first reaches its plateau. Which of the following best describes the error in this approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The EC50 should be placed on the linear portion of the curve

choices.label: B
choices.text: The EC50 should be read at the Emax plateau, so no error was made

choices.label: C
choices.text: The EC50 should be read at the highest concentration tested

choices.label: D
choices.text: The EC50 should be read from the linear-scale hyperbolic plot instead

choices.label: E
choices.text: The EC50 should be read where the curve meets the x axis

explanation.summary: A drug's EC50 must be determined on the linear portion of the sigmoidal curve, not at the plateau.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that it is very important to determine a drug's EC50 by placing it on a linear portion of the curve. The EC50 is the concentration producing 50% of the maximum response, which lies on the steep, linear middle segment of the sigmoid, not where the curve flattens at its maximum.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The plateau corresponds to Emax (maximal effect), not to the half-maximal concentration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The highest concentration tested lies in the saturated region and does not produce a half-maximal response.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The semi-log plot is the preferred method for determining EC50; the hyperbolic plot makes it harder.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Where the curve meets the x axis the effect is near zero, not 50% of maximum.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A new drug is designed to inhibit dopamine receptors. In cells expressing dopamine receptors, which of the following measured changes would confirm that the drug is producing its intended effect?

explanation.summary: A drug that inhibits dopamine receptors should have the effect of decreasing G protein activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that a drug's effect describes the downstream consequences of a drug-target interaction: a drug meant to activate dopamine receptors should increase G protein activity, whereas a drug meant to inhibit dopamine receptors should decrease G protein activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bronchodilation is the effect of beta-2 receptor activation by albuterol, unrelated to dopamine receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased G protein activity is the expected effect of a drug that activates dopamine receptors, the opposite of inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A drug blocking the receptor would not increase the maximal effect that dopamine can produce.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An inhibitor blocks receptor function; it is not expected to raise the receptor's affinity for dopamine.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A figure plots drug concentration in logarithmic form on the x axis and the measured effect on the y axis for two drugs. For each drug, the effect increases in proportion to the increase in dose until a maximum is reached. This plot is called which of the following?

explanation.summary: A plot of log drug concentration against effect, in which effect increases in proportion to dose, is a graded dose-response curve.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes a figure with log drug concentration on the x axis and effect on the y axis, where the drug effect increases in proportion to the increase in drug dose, and names it a graded dose-response curve. Efficacy and potency parameters are read from it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: EC50 is the half-maximal concentration read from the curve, not the plot itself.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Emax is the maximal effect read from the curve, not the name of the plot.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A Lineweaver-Burk plot is an enzyme kinetics plot, not a plot of drug effect versus log concentration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A Michaelis-Menten plot describes enzyme kinetics rather than drug effect versus dose.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: Two agonists at the same receptor are compared on a graded dose-response curve. Drug G reaches half of its own maximal effect at a concentration of 1 unit and plateaus at 70% of the reference response. Drug B reaches half of its own maximal effect at 10 units and plateaus at 100% of the reference response. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Drug B is more potent and also has greater efficacy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drug B is more potent, and drug G has greater efficacy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drug G is more potent and also has greater efficacy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drug G is more potent, and drug B has greater efficacy

choices.label: E
choices.text: The drugs have equal potency but differ in efficacy

explanation.summary: Potency is judged by EC50 (lower is more potent) and efficacy by Emax (higher is more efficacious); the two properties are independent.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the brick's figure, the drug with the higher Emax has more efficacy, while the drug that achieves its EC50 at a lower concentration is more potent because less drug is required for it to act. Drug G reaches its EC50 at 1 unit versus 10 units for drug B, so G is more potent; drug B plateaus higher, so B has greater efficacy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Drug B has greater efficacy, but its higher EC50 makes it less potent, not more.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Drug B needs a higher concentration (10 units) to reach its EC50, so it is less potent, and its Emax is the higher one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Drug G's plateau (70%) is lower than drug B's (100%), so G does not have greater efficacy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The EC50 values differ tenfold, so the potencies are not equal.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A medicinal chemist modifies an agonist so that it binds its receptor more tightly (lower Kd) without changing the maximal response it can produce. Assuming the usual relationship between affinity and potency applies, which of the following changes is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: EC50 and Emax both remain unchanged

explanation.summary: Higher affinity means more receptors occupied at lower concentration, so EC50 decreases and potency increases.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lays out the chain: higher affinity leads to more receptors being occupied (bound) at a lower concentration, which causes the EC50 to decrease, which means potency increases. A lower Kd reflects higher affinity, so the modified agonist is expected to have a lower EC50 and greater potency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Although Emax is unchanged, the higher affinity is expected to shift the EC50 lower.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A rise in EC50 with lower potency is the change expected from decreased affinity, not increased affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Emax was not altered by the modification; efficacy is unchanged.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The maximal response was stated to be unchanged, so Emax and efficacy do not increase.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: The extent or fraction to which a drug binds to its receptors at any given drug concentration, or how tightly the drug binds to the receptor, defines which of the following properties?

explanation.summary: Affinity is the extent of drug binding to receptors at a given concentration, or how tightly the drug binds.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines affinity as the extent or fraction to which a drug binds to receptors at any given drug concentration, or how tightly the drug binds to the receptor. Its matching exercise pairs 'extent of drug binding' with affinity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Efficacy is the maximal response a drug produces, not how tightly it binds.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Emax is the maximum effect of the drug, not a measure of binding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Potency is the amount of drug needed to reach an established effect (EC50), not the extent of binding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Selectivity describes producing one main effect at an appropriately high concentration, not binding extent.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: Drug X binds a receptor with a Kd of 5 nM and drug Y binds the same receptor with a Kd of 50 nM, yet on a graded dose-response curve their EC50 values are nearly identical. Which of the following best accounts for this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Affinity and potency are entirely unrelated properties

choices.label: B
choices.text: Affinity is only one of the factors that determine potency

choices.label: C
choices.text: EC50 is set by the Emax rather than by receptor binding

choices.label: D
choices.text: Higher affinity always raises rather than lowers the EC50

choices.label: E
choices.text: The lower Kd value must have been measured incorrectly

explanation.summary: Affinity is one factor that determines potency, but the affinity-to-potency relationship does not apply to all drugs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that affinity is one of the factors that determine potency and that higher affinity often increases potency, but it explicitly notes that this relationship is not always applicable to all drugs. Two drugs can therefore differ in Kd while having similar EC50 values.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Affinity is explicitly described as one of the factors determining potency, so they are related, just not perfectly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EC50 is the concentration producing 50% of Emax; it is not determined by the height of Emax.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Higher affinity tends to lower, not raise, the EC50 when the usual relationship holds.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no basis to assume a measurement error; the brick allows for affinity and potency to diverge.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with asthma relies on an albuterol rescue inhaler. She develops persistent tachycardia and requires a beta-blocker. Her physician chooses metoprolol rather than propranolol. Which of the following best explains this choice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Metoprolol activates beta-1 receptors rather than blocking them

choices.label: B
choices.text: Metoprolol binds beta-2 receptors with higher affinity than propranolol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Metoprolol spares beta-2 receptors, whereas propranolol blocks all beta receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Propranolol has a lower Emax than metoprolol at beta-1 receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Propranolol is specific for beta-1 receptors at any concentration

explanation.summary: Propranolol blocks all beta receptors, including the beta-2 receptors albuterol must activate; metoprolol selectively blocks beta-1.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes propranolol as a non-selective beta-blocker that blocks all beta receptors, and metoprolol as a selective beta-1 blocker used for increased heart rate. Because albuterol works by activating beta-2 receptors in the lungs to cause bronchodilation, a drug that blocks all beta receptors would interfere with that action, whereas the beta-1-selective metoprolol spares beta-2 receptors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Metoprolol is a beta-blocker (antagonist) at beta-1 receptors; it does not activate them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Metoprolol is chosen because it largely spares beta-2 receptors, not because it binds them more tightly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The distinction between the two drugs is selectivity, not a difference in maximal effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Propranolol is the non-selective agent that blocks all beta receptors; it is not beta-1 specific.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A patient taking a selective beta-1 blocker has the dose escalated for better rate control. At the higher dose, effects attributable to beta-2 receptor blockade begin to appear. Which of the following best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Selective drugs act on additional receptor sites at high concentrations

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drug has become specific for beta-1 receptors at the higher dose

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drug has converted from a competitive antagonist into a partial agonist

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drug's affinity for beta-1 receptors has decreased at the higher dose

choices.label: E
choices.text: The drug's Emax at beta-1 receptors has been exceeded by the higher dose

explanation.summary: Most drugs are selective rather than specific because they act on more than one receptor site once they reach an appropriately high concentration.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that the vast majority of drugs are selective rather than specific, because most drugs will act on more than one receptor site once they reach an appropriately high concentration. A selective beta-1 blocker given at high doses can therefore begin to block beta-2 receptors as well.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Specificity means one effect and only one effect on all biological systems; gaining a second effect is the opposite of becoming specific.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Raising the dose does not change a blocker into an activator; the new effects reflect blockade at another receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Affinity is a property of the drug-receptor interaction and is not lowered by raising the dose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Emax is a maximal response that cannot be exceeded; it does not explain new effects at another receptor.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with hypertension and a heart attack 5 years ago is reviewed before minor knee surgery. He takes lisinopril for hypertension, metoprolol to control his elevated heart rate, and aspirin to reduce clotting risk. Which of his medications produces its effect by blocking a receptor and preventing that receptor's associated cellular action?

explanation.summary: Metoprolol is a beta-blocker, a receptor antagonist that blocks beta-1 receptors to inhibit increases in heart rate.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes metoprolol as a selective beta-1 blocker, used to inhibit increases in heart rate. Blocking a receptor's function and its associated cellular action is the definition of an antagonist, so metoprolol is the receptor-blocking drug in his regimen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aspirin is presented as reducing clotting risk; the brick does not describe it as blocking a receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neither lisinopril nor aspirin is described as a receptor antagonist; only metoprolol is a beta-blocker.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lisinopril is presented as his hypertension medication; the brick does not describe it as a receptor blocker.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metoprolol is a beta-1 blocker, so at least one of his medications is a receptor antagonist.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A surgical resident meets with a 50-year-old man 3 weeks before his scheduled minor knee surgery to review his medications, which include aspirin. The resident explains that aspirin must be stopped 1 week before the surgery. For how much longer after this meeting should the patient continue taking aspirin?

choices.label: D
choices.text: He should continue it through the day of surgery

explanation.summary: With surgery 3 weeks away and aspirin stopped 1 week before surgery, aspirin continues for 2 more weeks.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the case, the resident meets the patient 3 weeks prior to surgery and states that aspirin is to be stopped 1 week (7 days) before the operation and restarted post-discharge. Counting from the meeting, the patient continues aspirin for 2 weeks and then stops for the final week before surgery.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Stopping after 1 week would leave a 2-week gap before surgery, not the 1 week described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Continuing for 3 weeks would mean taking aspirin up to the day of surgery, which the plan does not allow.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aspirin increases bleeding risk and is to be held for the week before surgery, not continued through it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stopping today would be 3 weeks before surgery, far earlier than the 1-week interval described.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: Receptors mediate the action of a drug. Which of the following is another role attributed to receptors in pharmacodynamics?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absorbing the drug from the gut into the bloodstream

choices.label: B
choices.text: Determining the selectivity of how the drug works

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excreting the drug in the urine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Metabolizing the drug into inactive products

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transporting the drug across the blood-brain barrier

explanation.summary: Receptors determine the dose-effect relationship, determine the selectivity of drug action, and mediate the drug's action.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that receptors determine the relationship between dosing a drug and its effect, determine the selectivity of how the drug works, and mediate the action of the drug. Selectivity is therefore a receptor-determined property.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absorption is a process of drug movement into the body, not a role of the receptor that mediates drug action.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Excretion removes the drug from the body and is not a receptor function.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metabolism is carried out by enzymes that break down drugs, not by the receptors described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transport across barriers is a distribution process, not one of the receptor roles described.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A neurotransmitter synthesized by the body and a drug administered by inhalation both bind the same receptor and activate it. Which of the following correctly classifies the two molecules?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both are endogenous ligands synthesized within the body

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both are exogenous ligands introduced from outside the body

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both are ligands, one endogenous and one exogenous

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only the drug is a ligand, because it is administered exogenously

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only the neurotransmitter is a ligand, because it is endogenous

explanation.summary: A ligand is any molecule that binds a receptor; ligands can be endogenous (made by the body) or exogenous (introduced from outside).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines a ligand as a molecule that binds to a receptor and states that ligands can be endogenous or exogenous to the body. The body's own neurotransmitter is an endogenous ligand, and the inhaled drug is an exogenous ligand; both bind and activate the receptor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The inhaled drug comes from outside the body, so it is exogenous, not endogenous.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The neurotransmitter is synthesized by the body and is therefore endogenous.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The neurotransmitter binds the receptor and is therefore also a ligand.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The drug also binds the receptor, so it is a ligand as well.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: In a semi-log dose-response plot, which of the following quantities is placed on the x axis?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drug concentration on a linear scale

explanation.summary: A semi-log plot places the logarithm of drug concentration on the x axis against effect on the y axis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the semi-log scale as the logarithm of drug concentration versus effect, and its graded dose-response figure plots drug concentration in logarithmic form on the x axis with the effect on the y axis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Kd is a single binding parameter, not an axis variable.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A linear concentration axis gives the hyperbolic plot, not the semi-log plot.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The effect is plotted on the y axis and is not log-transformed in a semi-log plot.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Receptor occupancy is not the x-axis variable of a dose-response plot.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: A researcher measures how tightly a series of ligands bind to the beta-2 receptor, independent of any cellular response the ligands might produce. Which of the following parameters is derived from these binding measurements?

explanation.summary: The dissociation constant (Kd) describes the strength of binding between a ligand and its receptor; affinity equals 1/Kd.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the strength of the binding (interaction) of a ligand or drug and its receptor is described by affinity, with Kd as the dissociation constant: the higher the Kd, the weaker the binding. Albuterol, for example, has a Kd of 100 nM for the beta-2 receptor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Efficacy is the maximal response produced, not the strength of binding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EC50 is the concentration producing 50% of the maximal effect, a response measure rather than a pure binding measure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Emax is the maximal effect of the drug, which requires measuring a response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Selectivity concerns which effects a drug produces at a given concentration, not binding strength.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: Albuterol is used in the treatment of asthma. Which of the following describes albuterol's drug effect, that is, the downstream consequence of the drug-target interaction, rather than the interaction itself?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acting as an agonist at the beta-2 receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binding to the beta-2 receptor with a Kd of 100 nM

choices.label: D
choices.text: Competing with the endogenous ligand for its binding site

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serving as an exogenous ligand for the receptor

explanation.summary: Drug effect is the downstream consequence of the drug-target interaction; for albuterol that is bronchodilation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines drug effect as the downstream consequences that occur after a drug-target interaction. Albuterol activates beta-2 receptors in the lungs (the interaction), and the resulting bronchodilation that opens the airways is its effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acting as an agonist describes how albuterol interacts with the receptor, not the effect that follows.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Binding with a Kd of 100 nM describes the affinity of the drug-receptor interaction, not its downstream consequence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Competing for the binding site describes antagonist behavior, and in any case is an interaction rather than an effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Being an exogenous ligand is a classification of the binding molecule, not a downstream effect.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: Two drugs bind the same receptor with identical Kd values and reach their half-maximal responses at the same concentration, yet at saturating concentrations drug 1 produces a substantially larger maximal response than drug 2. The two drugs differ in which of the following?

explanation.summary: Drugs binding the same receptor can differ in affinity and/or efficacy; a different maximal response with the same binding reflects a difference in efficacy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that drugs can bind to the same receptor but might differ in terms of their affinity and/or efficacy. Efficacy is the measure of the maximal response (Emax) produced by the drug, so a larger maximal response with identical binding parameters indicates greater efficacy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Affinity reflects Kd, which is identical for the two drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The dissociation constants are stated to be the same, so Kd cannot be what differs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Selectivity concerns acting on one main receptor site at an appropriate concentration, not the height of the response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Specificity refers to producing a single effect on all biological systems and is not defined by the size of the maximal response.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 1: Receptor Agonists and Antagonists

questions.stem: During a pharmacology lecture, a student is told that a certain antibiotic has a minimum effective concentration of 2 mg/L and a minimum toxic concentration of 9 mg/L. What is the size of this drug's therapeutic window?

explanation.summary: The therapeutic window is the range of plasma concentrations between the minimum effective concentration and the minimum toxic concentration.
explanation.whyCorrect: The therapeutic window spans from the minimum effective concentration (2 mg/L) up to the minimum toxic concentration (9 mg/L). Its size is therefore 9 - 2 = 7 mg/L, the range in which the drug is both effective and non-toxic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 2 mg/L is the minimum effective concentration itself, not the width of the window.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 4.5 mg/L is roughly the midpoint of the two values, not the range between them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 9 mg/L is the minimum toxic concentration, the upper boundary rather than the window size.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 11 mg/L is the sum of the two concentrations, which has no physiologic meaning here.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company is preparing to move a new compound from animal studies into first-in-human trials and wants to calculate the drug's margin of safety to help set the starting dose. Which pair of parameters is most appropriate for this calculation?

explanation.summary: The margin of safety compares the dose effective in nearly all subjects with the dose lethal to a very small fraction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The margin of safety is calculated as LD1 divided by ED99: it relates the dose that is therapeutic in 99% of animals to the dose that is lethal in just 1%. This preclinical measure is used to help set safe starting doses when moving into human trials.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ED50 and LD1 mixes a median effective dose with an extreme lethal dose and is not the defined ratio.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ED50 and LD50 are both median doses and do not capture the safety at the tails of the distributions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ED50 and TD50 give the therapeutic index, which uses median (50%) doses rather than the extremes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ED99 and TD50 pairs an extreme effective dose with a median toxic (not lethal) dose and is not used for margin of safety.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after swallowing a bottle of his mother's iron supplements. He is treated with deferoxamine, a chelator that binds free iron so it can be eliminated by the kidneys. This drug's action is best classified as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Chemical antagonism occurs when one substance directly binds and inactivates another without involving a receptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Deferoxamine directly binds (chelates) free iron to inactivate it and promote its elimination. This is chemical antagonism, in which one agent inactivates another through a direct chemical interaction rather than acting at a drug receptor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Competitive antagonism is reversible blockade at a shared receptor site, which does not describe metal chelation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An inverse agonist binds a receptor and produces an effect opposite to that of an agonist; no receptor is involved here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Irreversible receptor antagonism requires binding to a drug receptor; iron chelation involves no receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Physiologic antagonism involves two agents producing opposite effects through different physiologic pathways, not one binding the other.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman taking warfarin daily for atrial fibrillation must return to an anticoagulation clinic every week for blood testing and dose adjustment. Which property of warfarin best explains this need for frequent monitoring?

explanation.summary: Drugs with a narrow therapeutic index have effective and toxic concentrations close together and require close monitoring.
explanation.whyCorrect: Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic index, meaning its effective and toxic concentrations are in close proximity. Too little leaves the patient prone to clotting and too much causes bleeding, so plasma levels must be monitored weekly to keep the patient within the safe dosing window.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A high margin of safety implies a large gap between effective and harmful doses, which would not require frequent testing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A high median lethal dose alone would make a drug safer, not mandate weekly monitoring.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Low potency relates to the dose needed for an effect, not to the closeness of toxic and effective concentrations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A wide therapeutic window would reduce the need for monitoring, the opposite of warfarin's situation.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is found unconscious after accidentally injecting too much insulin. Paramedics administer glucagon, which raises his blood glucose by promoting glycogen breakdown and opposing insulin's glucose-lowering effect. The relationship between glucagon and insulin is an example of which of the following?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Competitive antagonism at a shared receptor

explanation.summary: Physiologic antagonism occurs when two agents produce opposite physiologic effects through different pathways.
explanation.whyCorrect: Insulin lowers blood glucose while glucagon raises it, each acting through its own pathway rather than a shared receptor. This opposing action on the same physiologic outcome is physiologic (functional) antagonism, which helps maintain glucose homeostasis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Additive agonism describes two agents acting in the same direction, whereas these hormones oppose each other.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chemical antagonism would require one hormone to directly bind and inactivate the other, which does not occur.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Insulin and glucagon act at their own distinct receptors, not a single shared receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A pharmacokinetic interaction alters absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion, not opposing physiologic effects.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: A new analgesic has a median effective dose (ED50) of 10 mg and a median toxic dose (TD50) of 250 mg. What is this drug's therapeutic index?

explanation.summary: The therapeutic index is the ratio of the median toxic dose to the median effective dose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Therapeutic index = TD50 / ED50 = 250 mg / 10 mg = 25. A larger value indicates a wider separation between toxic and effective doses and thus a relatively safer drug.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 0.04 is ED50 divided by TD50, the ratio inverted.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 240 is the difference between the two doses, not their ratio.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 260 is the sum of the two doses, which is not how the index is calculated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 2500 is the product of the two doses rather than their ratio.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: Two drugs, X and Y, relieve pain through the same receptor. On their graded dose-response curves, drug X reaches the same maximal effect as drug Y but does so at a lower concentration (its EC50 is smaller). Which statement best describes drug X compared with drug Y?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Drug X has a higher Emax than drug Y

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drug X has greater affinity but lower efficacy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drug X is more efficacious but less potent

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drug X is more potent but has equal efficacy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Drug X necessarily has a larger therapeutic index

explanation.summary: Potency is reflected by EC50, while efficacy is reflected by the maximal response (Emax).
explanation.whyCorrect: Because drug X produces its effect at a lower concentration (smaller EC50), it is more potent. Because it reaches the same maximal effect as drug Y, the two drugs have equal efficacy. Potency and efficacy are independent properties.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Emax is the maximal effect, which is equal for both drugs by the stem.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both drugs reach the same maximal response, so drug X does not have lower efficacy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Drug X reaches the same maximal effect, so it is not more efficacious; it is more, not less, potent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Therapeutic index depends on toxic and effective doses and cannot be inferred from potency alone.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: In comparing two drugs, a clinician notes that at very high doses drug A produces a greater maximal response than drug B. Which pharmacodynamic property distinguishes these two drugs?

explanation.summary: Efficacy is the ability of a drug to produce a maximum response.
explanation.whyCorrect: Efficacy describes the maximal effect a drug can produce, quantified by Emax. A drug that reaches a greater maximal response at high doses has greater efficacy; differences in efficacy are evaluated by comparing maximal responses at high doses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Affinity is how well a drug binds its receptor, not the magnitude of the maximal effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Margin of safety is a preclinical safety measure, unrelated to maximal effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Potency refers to the amount of drug needed for a given effect (compared by EC50), not the size of the maximal response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Therapeutic index is a safety ratio, not a measure of maximal response.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: During a lecture on drug-receptor interactions, a professor defines a property as the tenacity with which a drug binds to its receptor, a step that occurs before any downstream response is produced. Which property is being described?

explanation.summary: Affinity is how well, or how tightly, a drug binds to its receptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Affinity is defined as the tenacity with which a drug binds to its receptor. It describes the binding step itself; efficacy is what happens after the drug is bound to the receptor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Efficacy is the response produced after binding, not the binding itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Potency is the amount of drug needed for a given effect, compared using EC50 or ED50.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Selectivity refers to preference among different targets, not the strength of binding to one receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tolerance is a decreased response with repeated dosing, unrelated to binding tenacity.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: A researcher wants to determine the median dose of a drug that will cause hiccups within 6 hours in a large group of volunteers, recording only whether each person does or does not develop hiccups. Which type of dose-response relationship is being studied?

explanation.summary: Quantal dose-response curves measure all-or-none outcomes across a population.
explanation.whyCorrect: The outcome (hiccups) is present or absent in each individual and cannot be graded, and it is measured across a large population. This all-or-none, population-level relationship is a quantal dose-response study, which is used to determine a median effective dose such as the ED50 for causing hiccups.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Concentration-clearance describes elimination pharmacokinetics, not a quantal effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A graded dose-response curve plots a continuous effect against concentration in a single patient, not an all-or-none population outcome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Log-linear potency is not a defined dose-response study of a population outcome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A time-response relationship tracks effect over time, not the proportion of a population responding.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: Two antihypertensive drugs are compared. Drug P has a therapeutic index of 3, while drug Q has a therapeutic index of 40. Which of the following is the most accurate conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Drug P is more effective because it produces its benefit at a lower dose

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drug P requires less plasma level monitoring than drug Q does

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drug Q has a smaller therapeutic window between its effective and toxic doses

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drug Q has greater separation between its effective and toxic doses

choices.label: E
choices.text: Drug Q is more potent than drug P at equivalent doses

explanation.summary: A larger therapeutic index means less overlap between the effective and toxic dose-response curves, indicating greater relative safety.
explanation.whyCorrect: The therapeutic index reflects the separation between the toxic and effective doses. Drug Q's much larger index (40 versus 3) means its efficacy and toxicity curves overlap less, so it is relatively safer and generally needs less intensive monitoring.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The therapeutic index says nothing about which drug is more effective or works at a lower dose.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is reversed: drug P, with the narrow index of 3, requires more monitoring, not less.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A larger index generally corresponds to a wider, not smaller, margin between effective and toxic levels.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Potency is judged by EC50 or ED50, not by the therapeutic index.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: A physician starts a patient on the lowest dose of a drug that produces clinical benefit; below this plasma concentration the drug is ineffective. What is the term for this lowest concentration that provides a therapeutic effect?

explanation.summary: The minimum effective concentration is the lowest plasma concentration at which a drug shows clinical benefit.
explanation.whyCorrect: The minimum effective concentration is defined as the lowest plasma concentration at which a drug produces a clinical benefit; it forms the lower boundary of the therapeutic window. Below it, the drug is ineffective.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The median effective dose (ED50) is a population dose measure, not a plasma concentration threshold in one patient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The minimum toxic concentration is the level above which toxic effects appear, the upper boundary of the window.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peak plasma concentration is the highest level reached after a dose, not the minimum needed for effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Steady-state concentration is when input equals elimination, not specifically the threshold for benefit.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with frequent heartburn takes an over-the-counter antacid containing magnesium hydroxide and aluminum hydroxide. His symptoms improve because these basic compounds bind to stomach acid and neutralize it. This drug action is best classified as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Antacids are chemical antagonists: they neutralize stomach acid by a direct chemical reaction rather than acting at a receptor or enzyme.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chemical antagonism occurs when one agent interacts with and inactivates another by a specific chemical reaction apart from enzyme inhibition. Antacids such as sodium bicarbonate, magnesium hydroxide, and aluminum hydroxide are basic compounds that bind stomach acid and neutralize it, which is a classic example of a chemical inhibitor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Competitive receptor antagonism requires reversible binding at a shared receptor site; no receptor is involved in acid neutralization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chemical antagonism is specifically defined as occurring apart from enzyme inhibition; antacids do not inhibit an enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An inverse agonist binds a receptor and produces the opposite of the agonist's effect, which is not how antacids work.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Physiologic antagonism involves two agents producing opposite effects through different physiological systems, not direct neutralization of one substance by another.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with ovarian cancer is treated with cisplatin. The drug produces its effect by intercalating into DNA and causing damage, without binding to a specific cell-surface receptor or inhibiting an enzyme. Within the framework of antagonist mechanisms, cisplatin is best described as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Anticancer drugs such as cisplatin that intercalate into DNA to cause damage act as chemical inhibitors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chemical antagonism occurs when a drug inactivates its target by a specific chemical reaction apart from enzyme inhibition. Cisplatin intercalates directly into DNA to cause damage, so it acts through a direct chemical interaction rather than through a receptor or enzyme, making it a chemical inhibitor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chemical antagonism is defined as occurring apart from enzyme inhibition, and cisplatin does not act by inhibiting an enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Irreversible receptor antagonism requires binding to a drug receptor; the stem states no receptor is involved.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A partial agonist activates a receptor to produce a submaximal response, which is unrelated to DNA damage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A physiologic inhibitor produces the opposite physiologic effect of another agent through a different system, which does not describe DNA intercalation.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: A pharmacology textbook describes an interaction between two drugs as "functional antagonism." Which of the following statements best characterizes this type of interaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One agent accelerates the hepatic metabolism and renal clearance of the other agent

choices.label: B
choices.text: One agent covalently modifies the shared receptor so that the other agent can no longer bind to it

choices.label: C
choices.text: One agent inactivates the other directly through a specific chemical reaction in solution

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two agents compete reversibly for the same binding site on one receptor in one tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two agents produce opposite physiologic effects, usually through different physiological systems

explanation.summary: Functional antagonism is another name for physiologic antagonism, in which two drugs produce opposite effects through different systems.
explanation.whyCorrect: Physiologic antagonism, also known as functional antagonism, occurs when two drugs reduce the activity of an enzyme- or receptor-activated process by producing the opposite physiologic effect, usually acting on different physiological systems. These opposing effects are typically compensatory mechanisms useful in maintaining homeostasis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Altering metabolism and clearance is a pharmacokinetic interaction, not an opposing physiologic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Covalent modification that prevents binding describes irreversible receptor antagonism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inactivation of one agent by another through a specific chemical reaction is chemical antagonism, not functional antagonism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reversible competition for the same receptor site is competitive antagonism at a single receptor level.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: An in vitro study of a new bronchodilator in isolated airway tissue reports an EC50 of 4 nM. A separate clinical study of the same drug in 300 patients reports an ED50 of 0.5 mg/kg for relief of bronchospasm. Which of the following best describes the relationship between these two values?

choices.label: A
choices.text: EC50 is derived from a quantal population curve, whereas ED50 is derived from a graded concentration-effect curve

choices.label: B
choices.text: EC50 is the concentration producing 50% of the maximal graded effect, whereas ED50 is the dose at which 50% of a population responds

choices.label: C
choices.text: EC50 is the dose at which 50% of a population responds, whereas ED50 is the concentration producing 50% of the maximal graded effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: EC50 measures the drug's intrinsic efficacy, whereas ED50 measures the drug's affinity for its target receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: They describe the same underlying quantity, differing only in the units in which they are conventionally reported

explanation.summary: EC50 comes from a graded dose-response curve and is the concentration producing 50% of maximal effect; ED50 comes from a quantal curve and is the dose at which 50% of a population responds.
explanation.whyCorrect: The graded dose-response curve is used to determine Emax and EC50, the concentration producing 50% of the maximal effect, and is concerned with plasma drug concentration in a single patient or preparation. The quantal dose-response curve is used to generate the median effective dose, ED50, the dose at which 50% of the individuals in a population show the specified all-or-none effect. The EC50 should not be confused with the ED50.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This is backward: EC50 comes from the graded curve and ED50 from the quantal curve.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the definitions: ED50 is the population dose and EC50 is the concentration for half-maximal graded effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neither value directly measures affinity; EC50 relates to potency on a graded curve and ED50 to a population dose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The two values are conceptually different (graded effect magnitude versus population proportion), not the same quantity in different units.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: When describing administration of a drug to a patient, clinicians refer to the amount given as a "dose" rather than a "concentration," even though the drug's effect depends on its concentration at the target. Which of the following best explains this convention?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Doses are more precise than concentrations because they are weighed rather than assayed

choices.label: B
choices.text: Plasma concentrations cannot be measured accurately once a drug is administered

choices.label: C
choices.text: Receptor occupancy in tissues is determined by the administered dose alone

choices.label: D
choices.text: The concentration achieved in the body depends on factors such as distribution and metabolism

choices.label: E
choices.text: The dose and the resulting plasma concentration are numerically identical in vivo

explanation.summary: In patients we speak of dose because the concentration actually achieved depends on multiple pharmacokinetic factors.
explanation.whyCorrect: When a drug is given to a patient, the concentration achieved in the body will depend on multiple factors such as distribution or metabolism. Because the clinician controls the amount administered but not the resulting concentration directly, the concentration is usually referred to as a dose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The convention is not about measurement precision; it reflects that dose is what the clinician controls.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Plasma concentrations can be measured (drugs such as warfarin are monitored by blood testing); the issue is that concentration is not directly set by the prescriber.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Receptor occupancy depends on the concentration reached at the target, which is influenced by distribution and metabolism, not dose alone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dose and plasma concentration are not identical; distribution and metabolism separate them.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: Investigators give a range of doses of a new drug to a large group of volunteers and record, at each dose (mg/kg), the number of patients who develop a headache. They plot dose on the x-axis and the number of patients responding on the y-axis. Which of the following best describes the expected shape of this frequency curve?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Straight line rising through the origin

explanation.summary: Plotting dose against the number of patients responding yields a Gaussian frequency distribution (bell curve).
explanation.whyCorrect: In a quantal dose-response study, the x-axis is drug dose and the y-axis is the number of patients responding. Plotting dose against the number of patients responding generates a frequency curve that has a Gaussian distribution, i.e., a bell curve, with the median effective dose at its center.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An exponential decay describes elimination kinetics, not the distribution of responders across doses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A rectangular hyperbola describes a graded response plotted on a linear concentration scale, not a population frequency plot.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The sigmoidal shape appears only after the frequency responses are summed cumulatively and plotted on a log scale.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The number responding rises and then falls with dose rather than increasing linearly without limit.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: A pharmacologist has a bell-shaped frequency distribution showing the number of individuals who first respond at each dose of a drug. She sums the responses cumulatively at each dose and replots them against dose on a logarithmic scale. Which of the following best describes the resulting curve?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bell-shaped curve showing the number of subjects responding at each dose

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bimodal curve showing two separate responder populations

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rectangular hyperbola showing the response of a single patient

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sigmoidal curve showing the cumulative percentage of subjects responding

choices.label: E
choices.text: Straight line showing the rate of drug elimination over time

explanation.summary: Cumulative summation of quantal responses on a log dose scale produces a sigmoidal quantal dose-response curve.
explanation.whyCorrect: If the quantal responses in the frequency distribution are summated at a given dose on a log scale, the resulting cumulative distribution looks like a sigmoidal dose-response curve. This curve represents the percentage of subjects that showed the drug effect and is the quantal dose-response curve from which ED50 is read.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The bell-shaped curve is the original frequency distribution before cumulative summation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cumulative summation of a single Gaussian distribution yields one sigmoid, not a bimodal curve.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A single-patient graded response is not what results from summing population responses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Elimination over time is a pharmacokinetic plot unrelated to summing responders across doses.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company completes quantal dose-response studies for a new antiemetic and determines its ED50. Which of the following is the most direct use of this value?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calculating the drug's volume of distribution

choices.label: D
choices.text: Measuring the drug's affinity for its receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recommending a dose range for prescribing

explanation.summary: Knowing the ED50 helps clinicians anticipate drug effects and lets the manufacturer recommend a prescribing dose range.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ED50 is the dose at which 50% of individuals show the specified quantal effect. The utility of knowing ED50 is that it helps clinicians anticipate the drug effects and allows the drug manufacturer to recommend a dose range for prescribing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Volume of distribution is a pharmacokinetic parameter unrelated to the quantal effective dose.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Emax is determined from a graded dose-response curve, not from the population ED50.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The minimum toxic concentration is a plasma concentration threshold for toxicity, not derived from the ED50.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Affinity describes how tightly a drug binds its receptor and is not given by the ED50.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: In a dose-ranging study, 200 healthy volunteers each receive a single oral dose of a new drug. At a dose of 30 mg, exactly 100 of the volunteers develop nausea, an adverse effect of the drug. Which of the following terms best describes the 30-mg dose?

explanation.summary: The TD50 is the dose that produces a toxic effect in 50% of a population.
explanation.whyCorrect: Side effects from a drug are dose dependent. Similar to the ED50, the median toxic dose (TD50) is defined as the dose that produces a toxic effect in 50% of a population. Here 100 of 200 volunteers (50%) developed the toxic effect at 30 mg, so 30 mg is the TD50.

whyWrongByChoice.A: EC50 is a concentration producing half-maximal effect on a graded curve, not a population dose.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The ED50 is the dose at which 50% of subjects show the desired therapeutic effect, not an adverse effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The LD50 is the dose that is lethal to 50% of a population; nausea is toxicity, not death.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ED99 is the dose effective in 99% of subjects, used in the margin of safety calculation.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: For a single drug, quantal dose-response curves are constructed for its therapeutic effect, its toxic effect, and its lethal effect in the same population. Which of the following correctly orders the median doses from lowest to highest?

explanation.summary: The therapeutic curve lies to the left of the toxic curve, which lies to the left of the lethal curve, so ED50 < TD50 < LD50.
explanation.whyCorrect: Therapeutic effects occur at the lowest doses, toxic effects at higher doses, and lethal effects at the highest doses. If the dose is increased beyond the toxic dose it could possibly be lethally harmful, so the median lethal dose (LD50) lies above the median toxic dose (TD50), which lies above the median effective dose (ED50).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lethality occurs at doses beyond the toxic dose, so LD50 cannot lie below TD50.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This ordering is completely reversed, with death occurring at the lowest doses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Placing TD50 below ED50 would mean toxicity appears before benefit, which contradicts the ordering of the curves.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The therapeutic effect appears at the lowest doses, so ED50 cannot be the highest value.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index

questions.stem: During preclinical evaluation of a new sedative, investigators find that the efficacy curve is very steep while the toxicity curve is shallow, so the two quantal curves are not parallel. They calculate TD50 / ED50 = 10 but worry this value may overstate how well the drug separates effective doses from toxic doses at the extremes of the population. Which of the following parameters is designed to address this limitation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Margin of safety (LD1 divided by ED99)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Therapeutic window (minimum effective to minimum toxic concentration)

explanation.summary: The therapeutic index uses median doses and ignores curve slopes; the margin of safety compares the tails (ED99 and LD1) to account for non-parallel curves.
explanation.whyCorrect: The therapeutic index does not take into account the comparative slopes of the efficacy and toxicity curves. When the curves are not parallel, using the median dose does not account for different slopes. The margin of safety, calculated from animal studies as LD1 divided by ED99, compares the dose that is therapeutic in 99% of animals with the dose lethal in just 1%, capturing the overlap at the extremes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Emax describes the maximal graded response and has nothing to do with safety at population extremes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: LD50 is a single median value and has the same limitation as TD50 in ignoring slope.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A potency ratio compares how much of two drugs is needed for an effect, not the safety of one drug at the tails.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The therapeutic window is a range of plasma concentrations for dosing a patient; it does not address curve slopes in a population.

questions.topicName: Pharmacodynamics 2: Quantal Dose Response and Therapeutic Index
